table.text: First, participants had to search for passengers and subsequently deliver them to specific stores.

Participants were seated in a virtual house with bare walls, facing two transparent planes, with the task of ranking 15 desert survival items by dragging them from the left transparent plane to numbered placeholders on the right transparent plane.

Participants were instructed to shoot or withhold shooting at human-like avatars based on their appearance as soldiers (go targets) or civilians (no-go targets) under time pressure within a 1-second response window.

With the video game character continuously moving forward, participants had to navigate laterally to collect targets and avoid obstacles while simultaneously responding to color changes of the monster's jewel and the character's clothing.
Participants were assigned to one of three gaze-strategy groups based on fixation-pattern clustering across the 10 training days: target-focused, distributed, and color-cuefocused.

In the Free Wally game, participants were required to make strategic decisions aimed at rescuing a whale by directing water jets either to the left or right in order to displace humanoid agents from a hill while simultaneously managing limited resources and game-level temporal constraints.
Gamepad controls were perturbed with a 90° rotation for movement and elastic resistance for shooting, introducing unintuitive controls to which participants had to adapt.

As in the standard variant of Space Fortress, participants were required to navigate the spaceship between two hexagons by applying thrust, destroying the fortress, and avoiding the spaceship's destruction from fortress shells or hexagon collisions.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on controlled laboratory tasks with limited ecological validity.
Video games offer a middle ground between laboratory and real-world settings, combining intuitive interaction with experimental control.
This scoping review, reported according to PRISMA-ScR, characterizes video game paradigms used in event-related EEG research and relates their findings to canonical laboratory effects.
Database and supplementary searches identified 29 studies using 26 paradigms.
Most paradigms used custom-built games and required visuomotor navigation or targeting within continuous gameplay, and most analyses were time-locked to feedback events such as hits or collisions.

Findings showed selective convergence with laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, and for movement-related activity.
Evidence for errorand feedback-related components was more limited, while early sensory responses were rarely examined.

We discuss emerging patterns in the use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms, the correspondence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, and the methodological challenges of studying event-related activity during gameplay.

In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about neural responses during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.
Cognitive event-related EEG research has traditionally relied on highly controlled, trial-based laboratory tasks.

While such paradigms offer strong internal validity and reproducibility, their simplified structure and unintuitive dynamics limit their ability to capture the neural underpinnings of how humans naturally engage with complex, dynamic environments.
Moreover, many laboratory tasks are repetitive and abstract, which may reduce participant engagement and compromise data quality.

Increasingly, researchers emphasize the need for experimental paradigms that capture cognitive processes under more naturalistic and dynamic conditions (e.g., Shamay-Tsoory and Mendelsohn, 2019; Matusz et al., 2019; Huk et al., 2018; Wise et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Increasingly, researchers emphasize the need for experimental paradigms that capture cognitive processes under more naturalistic and dynamic conditions (e.g., Shamay-Tsoory and Mendelsohn, 2019; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Matusz et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Huk et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">Wise et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For EEG studies, however, increasing ecological validity presents a particular challenge.

Real-world settings offer little control and can introduce substantial measurement noise that reduces the reliability and interpretability of EEG signals, whereas naturalistic stimuli such as films can be presented under controlled laboratory conditions but lack the interactive demands that characterize many cognitive operations.
Video games provide a promising middle ground between these approaches (Allen et al., 2024; Brändle et al., 2022; Naselaris et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Video games provide a promising middle ground between these approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Allen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Brändle et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Naselaris et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, video games offer interactive environments that capture aspects of real-world complexity while being designed primarily for enjoyment.
Their intuitive interactions guide player behavior and sustain engagement, while their programmable nature can give researchers control over experimental variables and event timing.

By drawing on a broad range of human abilities, video games have become increasingly useful tools for studying perceptual, motor, and cognitive processes (e.g., Green and Bavelier, 2012; Bavelier et al., 2012; Anguera et al., 2013; Boot et al., 2008; Boot, 2015; Mishra et al., 2016; Bediou et al., 2018; Bavelier and Green, 2019; Dale et al., 2020).
text.formatted: By drawing on a broad range of human abilities, video games have become increasingly useful tools for studying perceptual, motor, and cognitive processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Green and Bavelier, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bavelier et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Anguera et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Boot et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Boot, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Mishra et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Bediou et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Bavelier and Green, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Dale et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly for event-related EEG research, gameplay generates continuous, time-resolved data of environmental events, player responses, and action outcomes, which provide opportunities to time-lock neural activity to meaningful events within an ongoing interactive task.
Yet, applying event-related EEG approaches to video gameplay raises methodological and interpretive challenges.

In conventional laboratory tasks, discrete stimuli, responses, and outcomes can be separated in time, their physical properties controlled, and their probabilities and magnitudes systematically varied.

During gameplay, events may instead emerge gradually within changing scenes, overlap with ongoing actions and other events, and acquire their probability and significance from the game state and the player's behavior.
These features complicate precise event marking, the separation of overlapping neural responses, and the distinction between effects of sensory properties and task relevance.
They also raise questions about how game-elicited activity relates to established laboratory EEG effects.

During continuous visuomotor control, for example, information about an impending error may become available before an outcome occurs, blurring conventional distinctions between response-related errors and external feedback.
Similarities in waveform or frequency band therefore require further functional evidence to establish correspondence with canonical components.
Addressing these challenges requires considering both how game events are defined and measured and how their neural responses depend on the demands and context of play.

While previous reviews have examined selected aspects of gaming and virtual reality in neuroscience (Palaus et al., 2017; Burelli and Dixen, 2024; Calvo-Morata et al., 2022; Vasiljevic and de Miranda, 2020; Bohil et al., 2011; Ninaus et al., 2014; Bailenson et al., 2025), cognitive eventrelated EEG research during video gameplay has not yet been the focus of a systematic synthesis.
text.formatted: While previous reviews have examined selected aspects of gaming and virtual reality in neuroscience <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Palaus et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Burelli and Dixen, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Calvo-Morata et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Vasiljevic and de Miranda, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Bohil et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Ninaus et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bailenson et al., 2025)</ref>, cognitive eventrelated EEG research during video gameplay has not yet been the focus of a systematic synthesis.

text.text: In this scoping review, we thus characterize the video game paradigms and in-game events used for event-related EEG analyses, summarize the associated neural findings, and relate them to canonical laboratory effects where possible.
We also identify recurring methodological challenges and illustrate, with examples from the reviewed studies, how they may be addressed.

In sum, this synthesis aims to guide the selection and design of game paradigms, inform expectations about the neural responses elicited during gameplay, and support their interpretation in light of established laboratory findings in future research in this emerging field.
The remainder of this work is structured as follows.
In the Methods section, we describe the eligibility criteria, search strategy, study selection, data charting, and synthesis approach.
In the Results section, we report the selection of studies, characterize the video game paradigms, and present the EEG findings for stimulus-related, response-related, and feedback-related events.

In the Discussion section, we consider patterns in the use of video game paradigms, examine correspondences with and departures from laboratory EEG effects, and address methodological challenges and recommendations.
We conclude with the review's limitations and directions for future research.

This review was carried out in line with the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological guidance for scoping reviews (JBI; Peters et al., 2020; Pollock et al., 2023) and is presented according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR; Tricco et al., 2018).

text.text: A scoping review approach was considered appropriate because our aim was to map an evolving and heterogeneous literature rather than address a narrowly defined question through quantitative synthesis (Munn et al., 2018; Tricco et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A scoping review approach was considered appropriate because our aim was to map an evolving and heterogeneous literature rather than address a narrowly defined question through quantitative synthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Munn et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Tricco et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Articles were deemed eligible if they reported original research conducted with healthy human participants using video game paradigms to examine event-related EEG correlates, with analyses focused on in-game events.

Eligible event-related EEG analyses encompassed both event-related potentials (ERPs) and time-frequency approaches assessing event-related changes in oscillatory power, including event-related desynchronization/synchronization (ERD/ERS) and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSP).
Only English-language, peer-reviewed journal articles were considered, and no limits were placed on publication date or participants' age, gender, or prior video game experience.

To identify appropriate paradigms, we adopted the video game definition proposed by Allen et al. (2024), which focuses on virtual tasks that offer an interactive setting that is straightforward to engage with.
text.formatted: To identify appropriate paradigms, we adopted the video game definition proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Allen et al. (2024)</ref>, which focuses on virtual tasks that offer an interactive setting that is straightforward to engage with.

text.text: However, given the fundamentally subjective nature of enjoyment, we relaxed Allen et al. (2024)'s criterion that entertainment must be the video game's primary purpose.
text.formatted: However, given the fundamentally subjective nature of enjoyment, we relaxed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Allen et al. (2024)</ref>'s criterion that entertainment must be the video game's primary purpose.

text.text: We thus included paradigms that were video game-like in the sense that they were intuitive, interactive, and contained at least a potential element of enjoyment that made the activity intrinsically engaging, regardless of whether entertainment was the primary design goal.

To maintain comparability with standard laboratory tasks, we excluded studies using exergames, that is, games incorporating physical activity as a core gameplay element, and video games requiring movement beyond button presses, display taps, or joystick control.
We excluded studies focused on EEG responses to externally delivered haptic stimuli.
Mechanical resistance used to modify gamepad controls was not itself an exclusion criterion when the EEG analyses concerned players' actions or in-game events.

We also excluded studies using brain-computer interfaces (BCI) or other biofeedback systems in which neural or physiological signals, rather than deliberate participant responses, were used to control or modify the video game.

Studies that used a BCI system but recorded EEG passively during normal gameplay controlled by deliberate participant actions were included if they reported event-related EEG analyses, irrespective of whether the broader research project involved BCI development.

We further excluded studies conducted in neurofeedback settings or involving any form of electrical, magnetic, or ultrasound stimulation of the brain or any other body part, as neither the use of biosignals to control virtual environments nor interventions altering neural activity fall within the scope of this review.

To ensure methodological consistency across studies, we included studies using standard EEG systems or dry electrodes integrated into VR headsets, and excluded studies using intracranial EEG or mobile EEG systems.

Finally, we excluded studies examining inter-brain connectivity or synchrony, as the complexity of associated social-interaction processes exceeds the scope of this review, which focuses on the cognitive processes of individuals.
To identify eligible articles, we searched PubMed and Web of Science.
The initial search was conducted in February 2025.
To keep the review up to date during manuscript preparation and revision, we conducted a second search in June 2026.

Both searches were conducted by the first author and combined keywords referring to event-related EEG and variants of video game as follows: ((EEG) OR (electroencephalography) OR (ERP)) AND (video games OR videogame OR video-game OR videogaming OR video gaming OR computer game OR computergame OR computer-game OR computergaming OR computer gaming OR virtual reality game OR VR game OR virtual reality-game OR virtual reality gaming).
Results from PubMed and Web of Science were combined into a single table and duplicate records were removed.
These database searches were supplemented by Google Scholar searches and manual screening of the reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews.
The screening and selection of eligible studies from all unique records were conducted manually and independently by the first two authors.
Disagreements were resolved through discussion, with continuous consultation from the third author.
This process comprised three stages, during which the inclusion and exclusion criteria were iteratively refined.
We screened titles, abstracts, and full texts sequentially.

Full-text screening focused primarily on the Methods and Results to establish whether EEG was recorded during active gameplay, analyses were event-related, and paradigms met our operational definition of a video game.
Data from selected studies were extracted using a standardized data-charting form, developed collaboratively by the first and third authors, and summarized in a table.
Data charting was primarily conducted by the first author, with the continuous involvement of the third author.
Any uncertainties regarding study methods, procedures, analyses, or reported findings were discussed among the authors and resolved by consensus.
The form was refined iteratively throughout the review process as additional relevant aspects emerged during extraction.
The final charting form, along with all charted data, is available in the PsychArchives repository (https://doi.org/10.23668/psycharchives.22650.
text.formatted: The final charting form, along with all charted data, is available in the PsychArchives repository (<ref type="url" target="https://doi.org/10.23668/psycharchives.22650">https://doi.org/10</ref>.

text.text: Extracted data items covered the characteristics of each study, the video game employed, EEG recording and analysis procedures, and the study's key findings.

Because the included studies employed heterogeneous paradigms and methods, we synthesized their findings qualitatively in a narrative review, following best-practice guidelines (Siddaway et al., 2019) and the JBI methodological guidance for scoping reviews (Peters et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Because the included studies employed heterogeneous paradigms and methods, we synthesized their findings qualitatively in a narrative review, following best-practice guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Siddaway et al., 2019)</ref> and the JBI methodological guidance for scoping reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Peters et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In our narrative review, we first characterize the video game paradigms (Section 3.2) using the classification scheme outlined in Section 2.5.1, which distinguishes a paradigm's development origin, task requirements, gameplay organization, and presentation format.

We then organize the corresponding event-related EEG findings by stimulus-related, response-related, and feedbackrelated in-game events (Section 3.3), following the grouping principles and terminology outlined in Section 2.5.2.
We relate these findings to canonical event-related EEG effects where possible.

In the Discussion, we synthesize patterns in the use of video game paradigms, examine convergence and divergence between game-elicited and laboratory EEG effects, address methodological challenges and recommendations, and consider the review's limitations and directions for future research.
Overall, we use the term video game to refer to the game itself and the term video game paradigm to refer to the game-based task as implemented for research.
Distinct task variants of the same game are counted as separate paradigms, whereas repeated use or reanalysis of the same variant is not.

Along with its development origin (custom-built vs. commercial), we characterized each video game paradigm by its task requirements, gameplay organization, and presentation format to capture both a game's behavioral demands and its properties with relevance to experimental design in event-related EEG studies.
As the range of games could not be anticipated, all categories, particularly the task requirements, were derived inductively during data charting.

A game's task requirements are meant to capture the predominant behavioral demands on which successful performance depends: decision-making requires probabilistic or strategic choices among alternatives, go/no-go requires executing or withholding responses contingent on discriminative stimuli, spatial search requires identifying and approaching goal-relevant objects in a virtual environment, spatial puzzle-solving requires arranging visuospatial patterns, and visuomotor navigation and/or targeting requires the spatially accurate and well-timed execution of actions, such as steering, dodging, or aiming.

Two further requirements, first-person-shooter (FPS) combat and team combat, capture combat-centered gameplay in complex, richly rendered environments with human-like characters and realistic or narrative settings.
These combine demands such as navigation, strategic decisions, and coordination with teammates.
We note that games often combine several task requirements.
We therefore coded only the demands that primarily determined performance, rather than processes shared by most games or insufficiently described in the original studies.

We also report each game's closest commercial genre for orientation, but focus our synthesis on task requirements because games within the same genre can engage markedly different cognitive and motor processes.
We characterized gameplay organization using three features, each coded as present or absent.
Bounded epochs denote a trial-like structure of clearly delimited decision or action epochs, in contrast to continuous gameflow in which events unfold within an ongoing stream of play.
We classified responses as self-paced when players chose when to initiate individual actions, without an imperative cue or a prescribed response deadline.
Finally, we coded concurrent demands when players pursued two or more independent objectives simultaneously.

We distinguished these at a coarse, attentional level: navigating around obstacles while separately shooting at targets counted as two demands, whereas the perceptual, motor, and timing demands jointly required for a single task, such as aiming, did not count separately.
Finally, we classified a game's presentation format by visual format and player perspective.

Two-dimensional (2D) games included interface displays (abstract visual elements, such as geometric shapes or symbols, without environmental context), side views (lateral perspectives, including horizontally scrolling environments and static profile views, in which players navigate through a landscape), and displays with simulated depth, which used visual cues to suggest depth within a 2D display.

We further differentiated three-dimensional (3D) games, which allow movement along three spatial dimensions without immersive technology, and virtual reality (VR) games that use a head-mounted display.
text.formatted: We further differentiated three-dimensional (3D) games, which allow movement along three spatial dimensions without immersive technology, and virtual reality <ref type="bibr">(VR)</ref> games that use a head-mounted display.

text.text: For 3D games, we distinguish between top-down (bird'seye), third-person (positioned behind or above the player character), and first-person (aligned with the character's visual field) perspectives.
For VR games, we distinguish between a first-or third-person view.
To synthesize the event-related EEG findings, we grouped them according to whether the signals were time-locked to stimulus-related, response-related, or feedback-related video game events.

This grouping reflects neurocognitive models that describe information processing as a perception-action cycle spanning sensory input, behavioral output, and accompanying performance monitoring (Fuster, 2002 (Fuster, , 2004;; Badre, 2025; Botvinick et al., 2001; Ullsperger et al., 2014b).
text.formatted: This grouping reflects neurocognitive models that describe information processing as a perception-action cycle spanning sensory input, behavioral output, and accompanying performance monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Fuster, 2002</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Fuster, , 2004;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Badre, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ullsperger et al., 2014b)</ref>.

text.text: It also corresponds to the event categories commonly distinguished in event-related EEG research.
We define stimulus-related events broadly to include both discrete stimulus presentations, as in conventional laboratory tasks, and unexpected changes within the video game environment.
Response-related events comprise participant-initiated actions, such as button presses or joystick movements.
Feedback-related events signal the rewarding or punishing consequences of players' actions or performance.
Such feedback may take the form of explicit outcome displays or arise directly from gameplay, for example when an action results in a successful hit, a collision, or the loss of a life.
We present these three groups sequentially, while acknowledging that the underlying cognitive processes may overlap and interact rather than follow a strict temporal order.
Within each group, we organized the findings around the cognitive functions investigated or the sensitivity of neural responses to psychologically relevant properties of game events.
Where possible, we related these findings to canonical event-related EEG components and their established laboratory modulations (cf.
Supplementary Material S1).

Note that we use the term canonical event-related EEG component to denote well-known and commonly assessed event-related EEG effects that have been studied extensively and are covered in standard textbooks and reviews (e.g., Luck and Kappenman, 2011; Luck, 2014; Polich, 2007; Schomer and Lopes da Silva, 2017).
text.formatted: Note that we use the term canonical event-related EEG component to denote well-known and commonly assessed event-related EEG effects that have been studied extensively and are covered in standard textbooks and reviews (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b161">Luck and Kappenman, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Luck, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Schomer and Lopes da Silva, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For ease of presentation, we use shortened labels for commonly numbered ERP components (e.g., N1 instead of N100 and P3 instead of P300).
We retain N400, subcomponent labels such as P3a and P3b, and the original designation P300-CE.
Components reported as FN are labeled FRN.
These conventions apply to the main text, tables, and Supplementary Material.

Because component latencies, electrode sites, and spectral frequency ranges varied across studies, we report these alongside the corresponding findings in the overview tables wherever the original reports provided this information.

text.text: Systematic searches of PubMed and Web of Science yielded a total of 1,250 unique records after the removal of 460 duplicates (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Systematic searches of PubMed and Web of Science yielded a total of 1,250 unique records after the removal of 460 duplicates (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Throughout screening, many records met more than one exclusion criterion, so the counts reported below are not mutually exclusive.
Title and abstract screening excluded 877 records.

The most common reasons were pathologyrelated investigations (n = 315), BCI research (n = 253), non-empirical publication types (n = 154), and not meeting the operational definition of a video game (n = 98).

Further records primarily addressed neurofeedback (n = 41), exergames (n = 22), or hyperscanning (n = 18), lacked EEG data (n = 46), involved electrical, magnetic, or ultrasound stimulation of the brain or other body regions (n = 23), recorded EEG outside of active gameplay (n = 12), or were not available in English (n = 6 ).

An additional 33 records were excluded for other reasons, including biofeedback, drug manipulations, non-human participants, intracranial recordings, inter-brain connectivity or synchrony, and atypical game-control methods.
Of the 373 records retained for full-text assessment, one could not be retrieved, and 344 of the remaining 372 were excluded, yielding 28 eligible studies.
One additional eligible study was identified through supplementary Google Scholar searches and manual screening of reference lists.
The largest group of excluded records (n = 186) did not report event-related EEG data or did not time-lock such data to in-game events.

A second substantial group (n = 114) either did not use a video game at all, for instance comparing video game players and non-players on behavioral or neural measures obtained outside of gameplay, or used a task labeled as a "video game" or "computer game" that did not meet our operational definition.

Such tasks included minimally gamified cognitive tasks, economic games (e.g., the Ultimatum or Dictator game), social dilemma games (e.g., the Prisoner's dilemma), and other tasks with simple, static stimuli.

Gamified cognitive tasks were nonetheless retained if they exhibited more pronounced game-like characteristics, such as intuitive interaction, visual environments resembling commercial games, or immersive simulations of real-world scenarios.

Further records focused primarily on EEGbased classification or pattern recognition without reporting conventional event-related EEG outcomes (n = 48), or recorded EEG only before or after gameplay, or not at all (n = 35).

An additional 73 records were excluded for other reasons, such as a primary focus on connectivity analyses, the use of exergames, a focus on EEG responses to externally delivered haptic stimuli, or atypical game-control interfaces.
Across the 29 studies included, 26 unique video game paradigms were identified, as several paradigms were used or reanalyzed in more than one publication.

An overview of game characteristics and associated EEG measures is provided in Figure 2, with paradigms ordered by their predominant task requirements and their closest commercial genres shown alongside their names.

Within this group, control demands ranged from comparatively simple, quickly learned inputs, such as single-button tapping or one-dimensional steering (e.g., Pei et al., 2025; Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021), to multi-effector control requiring extended practice (e.g., Maclin et al., 2011; Mariman et al., 2023).

text.text: The paradigms also differed in the complexity of their gameplay.

At one end of this range were games built around repetitive, score-based actions, as in target-shooting tasks (e.g., Figure 3H), a paddle game (Pong; Rebert et al., 1984), or an endless runner (Flappy Bird ; Pei et al., 2025).

text.text: Others combined navigation with target collection or shooting (Figure 3E-G and I), or were platform games, in which players steer a character across elevated platforms while collecting rewards and avoiding hazards (Salminen and Ravaja, 2007; McMahan et al., 2015).

text.text: The remaining task requirements were rarely the primary demands.
Decision-making was the central demand in three paradigms (e.g., Figure 3A) and go/no-go in two, one with a trial-based (Figure 3B) and one with a continuous format (Figure 3C).

text.text: Spatial search (Figure 3D) and spatial puzzle-solving (Tetris; Bernal et al., 2024) were each represented by a single paradigm.
text.formatted: Spatial search (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3D</ref>) and spatial puzzle-solving (Tetris; <ref type="bibr">Bernal et al., 2024)</ref> were each represented by a single paradigm.

text.text: Beyond their predominant requirements, many games involved further demands that did not primarily determine performance and were therefore not coded separately.
The spatial search game, for instance, required players to navigate through a virtual town, but its central task goal was finding goal-relevant stores rather than navigating precisely.
Conversely, several visuomotor games required players to fire only at certain targets, which implicitly involves target search and response inhibition, but neither constituted the central task goal.

Notably, all games centered on decision-making, go/no-go, spatial search, or spatial puzzle-solving were custom-built, whereas all commercial titles involved visuomotor navigation and/or targeting, three of which also involved FPS or team combat.
Six paradigms organized gameplay into bounded epochs (e.g., Figure 3A, B and H), comprising two decision-making, one go/no-go, and three navigation and/or targeting paradigms.
text.formatted: Six paradigms organized gameplay into bounded epochs (e.g., Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>, B and H), comprising two decision-making, one go/no-go, and three navigation and/or targeting paradigms.

text.text: Only three paradigms, two decision-making and one navigation and/or targeting paradigm, allowed self-paced responses, meaning that players could choose the timing of individual responses.

In the others, movement was often self-paced in a broad sense, in that players could typically move through the environment at will, but discrete responses were reactive, their timing constrained by the appearance or approach of targets, tokens, or enemies.
Twelve paradigms required players to manage two or more concurrent demands, typically navigation combined with shooting.
All of these also involved navigation and/or targeting requirements.

Presentation formats ranged from 2D displays (n = 12), including displays with simulated depth and those depicting abstract geometric forms (e.g., Figure 3E) or minimalist but thematically contextualized scenes (e.g., Figure 3F and G), to 3D environments, presented from a top-down view (n = 2, e.g., Figure 3B), a first-or third-person perspective on a standard screen (n = 6, e.g., Figure 3B and D), or in immersive VR with a first-or third-person perspective (n = 7, e.g., Figure 3C, H and I).

text.text: Of the 29 included studies, 10 reported EEG activity time-locked to stimulus-related events, 6 to response-related events, and 18 to feedback-related events.

Twenty studies reported ERPs, 14 reported time-frequency analyses of event-related spectral power changes (including ERD/ERS and ERSP), and 6 reported other EEG analyses, such as hemispheric asymmetry indices, timelocked power estimates, or EEG-based classification.
These categories are not mutually exclusive because several studies analyzed more than one event type or measure.
Figure 2 summarizes event locking and EEG measures at the paradigm level, counting paradigms used in multiple studies only once.

text.text: Stimulus-locked analyses predominated among the seven paradigms centered on decision-making, go/no-go, spatial search, or puzzle-solving (5 of 7), whereas feedback-locked analyses predominated among paradigms with visuomotor requirements (15 of 20).
Below, we present the findings separately for stimulus-, response-, and feedback-related events.

Stimulus-related events varied considerably in modality, response demands, and role within gameplay (Table 1).

text.text: Notably, early sensory processing was rarely examined, with only isolated reports of P1 or N1 effects (Petras et al., 2016; Wimmer et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Notably, early sensory processing was rarely examined, with only isolated reports of P1 or N1 effects <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wimmer et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This scarcity may partly reflect the research questions of the reviewed studies, most of which targeted later components, but also the experimental demands of early sensory analyses.

Early visual components are highly sensitive to physical stimulus properties such as luminance and contrast (Luck, 2014), which are difficult to control against the continuous visual change characteristic of video games.
text.formatted: Early visual components are highly sensitive to physical stimulus properties such as luminance and contrast <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Luck, 2014)</ref>, which are difficult to control against the continuous visual change characteristic of video games.

text.text: Moreover, analyses of early visual components are particularly susceptible to temporal imprecision introduced by manual event marking (e.g., Shin et al., 2012) or low game refresh rates (e.g., Maclin et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Moreover, analyses of early visual components are particularly susceptible to temporal imprecision introduced by manual event marking (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Shin et al., 2012)</ref> or low game refresh rates (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Maclin et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: To date, event-related EEG research using video game paradigms thus appears to have focused predominantly on later, largely endogenous components, even when time-locking EEG activity to basic stimulus onsets.
Rather than examining early sensory processing, the studies reviewed primarily addressed the role of stimuli within gameplay.

In this regard, we identified three clusters of stimulus-related events of interest: (1) stimuli that convey goal-relevant information, (2) stimuli that prompt response selection, and (3) stimuli that signal changes in the conditions of ongoing play.

(1) Stimulus events conveying goal-relevant information Two studies examined event-related changes in spectral power during the processing of information encountered in gameplay, focusing on its relevance to current goals or its mode of presentation.
In a taxi-driving game (Figure 3D), participants searched for passengers and delivered them to designated stores.
text.formatted: In a taxi-driving game (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3D</ref>), participants searched for passengers and delivered them to designated stores.

text.text: Frontal theta power decreased more for target stores than for neutral or non-target stores, consistent with a role in goal-directed object recognition and categorization (Weidemann et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Frontal theta power decreased more for target stores than for neutral or non-target stores, consistent with a role in goal-directed object recognition and categorization <ref type="bibr">(Weidemann et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Stores emerged gradually during navigation, so stimulus onset was operationalized as the moment a store occupied 0.35% of the display area, a threshold at which target stores were being directly approached on 95% of trials.
Because stores were distinguished by their relevance to the current destination rather than by their visual features, this contrast points to higher-order rather than perceptual processing.
In a VR decision-making task involving a virtual agent, alpha-band ERD/ERS time-locked to speech onset varied with communication modality (Chang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In a VR decision-making task involving a virtual agent, alpha-band ERD/ERS time-locked to speech onset varied with communication modality <ref type="bibr">(Chang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Embodied agents elicited parietal and occipital alpha ERS, gestural agents elicited ERD at both sites, and voice-only agents produced parietal ERD and occipital ERS.
The authors attributed these differences to greater speech-onset predictability when the agent's body was visible and to additional attentional demands imposed by sudden gesturing.

Although consistent with the association between alpha ERD and attentional engagement, this interpretation remains qualified by the joint variation of communication modality and predictability, particularly because anticipatory alpha ERD can itself be modality-specific (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017, cf.
Supplementary Material S1).

(2) Stimulus events prompting response selection Four studies examined stimulus events that required players to select or withhold a response according to task rules, including go/no-go cues and memory probes.

Three embedded go/nogo contingencies in video games and reported N2 and P3 components associated with response requirements, task performance, and training (Petras et al., 2016; Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026).
text.formatted: Three embedded go/nogo contingencies in video games and reported N2 and P3 components associated with response requirements, task performance, and training <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sanuki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiao and Iramina, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In laboratory tasks, no-go stimuli typically elicit a larger N2 than go stimuli, commonly associated with response inhibition or conflict (Folstein and Van Petten, 2008; Donkers and van Boxtel, 2004, cf.
text.formatted: In laboratory tasks, no-go stimuli typically elicit a larger N2 than go stimuli, commonly associated with response inhibition or conflict <ref type="bibr">(Folstein and Van Petten, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Donkers and van Boxtel, 2004, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
Only Petras et al. (2016)directly compared these conditions, finding a larger N2 to no-go than go targets in a virtual shooting scenario (Figure 3B).
text.formatted: Only <ref type="formula">Petras et al. (2016)</ref>directly compared these conditions, finding a larger N2 to no-go than go targets in a virtual shooting scenario (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3B</ref>).

text.text: The N2 was also larger when human-like targets appeared close in a first-person perspective than in a distant, bird's-eye view.
The authors attributed this difference to heightened moral conflict, although perceived distance was confounded with target size and visual complexity.

The other two studies used the same VR multitasking game (Figure 3C), in which participants navigated an environment while monitoring color changes in a monster's jewel and their avatar's clothing, responding when the colors differed (go) and withholding a response when they matched (no-go).
text.formatted: The other two studies used the same VR multitasking game (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3C</ref>), in which participants navigated an environment while monitoring color changes in a monster's jewel and their avatar's clothing, responding when the colors differed (go) and withholding a response when they matched (no-go).

text.text: Successful go, successful no-go, and failed no-go trials elicited N2 and P3 components, whereas failed go trials showed an attenuated N2 and no P3, suggesting that the cues had not been registered (Sanuki et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Successful go, successful no-go, and failed no-go trials elicited N2 and P3 components, whereas failed go trials showed an attenuated N2 and no P3, suggesting that the cues had not been registered <ref type="bibr">(Sanuki et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Training-related changes depended on gaze strategy: participants who primarily fixated the target field and perceived the color cues parafoveally developed enhanced no-go N2 and P3 components, whereas those who directly fixated the cues showed a reduced go P3 (Qiao and Iramina, 2026).
text.formatted: Training-related changes depended on gaze strategy: participants who primarily fixated the target field and perceived the color cues parafoveally developed enhanced no-go N2 and P3 components, whereas those who directly fixated the cues showed a reduced go P3 <ref type="bibr">(Qiao and Iramina, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The authors interpreted these patterns as increased conflict-monitoring demands for indirectly attended no-go cues and more efficient processing of directly attended go cues, respectively.

Memory-based response selection was examined in the standard variant of Space Fortress, in which players navigated a spaceship, attacked a fortress with correctly timed shots, and avoided damage (Maclin et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Memory-based response selection was examined in the standard variant of Space Fortress, in which players navigated a spaceship, attacked a fortress with correctly timed shots, and avoided damage <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Alongside these ongoing tasks, players classified appearing mines as friend or foe.
Each mine served as a memory probe because its letter code had to be compared with a previously memorized set of codes to determine the appropriate response.
The study combined gameplay with an auditory oddball task to test whether practice reduced attentional demands.

Reduced demands were expected to yield a smaller P3 to game events and a larger P3 to oddball tones, reflecting a reallocation of attentional resources (Isreal et al., 1980; Kramer et al., 1985; Polich, 2007, cf.
text.formatted: Reduced demands were expected to yield a smaller P3 to game events and a larger P3 to oddball tones, reflecting a reallocation of attentional resources <ref type="bibr">(Isreal et al., 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polich, 2007, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
Unlike the P3 to feedback-related events in the same study (Section 3.3.3), the mine-onset P3 did not decrease with training and tended to increase.

The authors attributed this persistence to changes across blocks in which letter codes identified foes, requiring players to continue consulting the memorized codes rather than relying on an automatized response.

(3) Stimulus events signaling changes in the conditions of ongoing play Four studies examined events that changed ongoing gameplay by perturbing control, interrupting visual continuity, or reducing task difficulty.

Two introduced unexpected perturbations of visuomotor control, either brief deviations of cursor movement in an obstacle-avoidance game (Spüler and Niethammer, 2015) or glider rotations and target displacements in a VR flight simulation (Wimmer et al., 2024, Figure  3I).
text.formatted: Two introduced unexpected perturbations of visuomotor control, either brief deviations of cursor movement in an obstacle-avoidance game <ref type="bibr">(Spüler and Niethammer, 2015)</ref> or glider rotations and target displacements in a VR flight simulation <ref type="bibr">(Wimmer et al., 2024, Figure</ref>  <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3I</ref>).

text.text: Both reported a similar frontocentral ERP sequence following perturbation onset: an early positivity, a negativity at 220-300 ms, a positivity at approximately 300-400 ms, and a later negativity at 400-500 ms.
The perturbations were designed to elicit system-generated errors, with potential applications in online error correction and system adaptation.

Accordingly, both studies interpreted the early negativity and subsequent positivity within an error-processing framework, as ERN/FRN-and Pe-like activity reflecting detection of, and adjustment to, externally generated errors (cf.
Supplementary Material S1).
A comparable ERP sequence followed brief display freezes in a VR slingshot game, introduced to investigate disruptions of presence (Center et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A comparable ERP sequence followed brief display freezes in a VR slingshot game, introduced to investigate disruptions of presence <ref type="bibr">(Center et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, comparison with normal trials, in which the released ball continued along its expected trajectory, showed that only the P3b and N400 differed: freezes reduced the P3b and enlarged the N400, whereas N2 amplitude remained unchanged.
The authors related the attenuated P3b to interrupted extraction of goal-relevant information and context updating, and the enlarged N400 to a violation of environmental coherence.

This interpretation extends the N400's classical association with semantic incongruence (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011) to expectancy violations concerning the physical behavior of the virtual environment (cf.
text.formatted: This interpretation extends the N400's classical association with semantic incongruence <ref type="bibr">(Kutas and Hillyard, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kutas and Federmeier, 2011)</ref> to expectancy violations concerning the physical behavior of the virtual environment (cf.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
A different change in gameplay was examined in a custom-built VR adaptation of Tetris, where an occasional helper piece cleared four rows and slowed the game (Bernal et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A different change in gameplay was examined in a custom-built VR adaptation of Tetris, where an occasional helper piece cleared four rows and slowed the game <ref type="bibr">(Bernal et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Spectral power changes around the clearing of rows were interpreted as reflecting reduced mental and visuospatial workload.
Frontal alpha and frontoparietal beta power increased before the event, whereas parietal alpha decreased and parietal beta increased afterward, followed by a later decrease in frontal theta.

The introduction of distinct helper pieces among standard tetrominos resembles an oddball manipulation, for which infrequent targets have been associated with alpha suppression (Yordanova et al., 2001, cf.
text.formatted: The introduction of distinct helper pieces among standard tetrominos resembles an oddball manipulation, for which infrequent targets have been associated with alpha suppression <ref type="bibr">(Yordanova et al., 2001, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
However, helper-piece frequency was not reported, and appearance depended on stack height.
Although this triggering rule was not disclosed, players may have learned it through experience, leaving the rarity and unexpectedness of these events uncertain.
Six studies reported EEG activity time-locked to response-related events, including key or button presses, trigger releases, and thumbstick displacement onsets (Table 2).
text.formatted: Six studies reported EEG activity time-locked to response-related events, including key or button presses, trigger releases, and thumbstick displacement onsets (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Compared with the diverse stimulus-related events, these response events and the processes examined had more direct counterparts in traditional laboratory EEG research, particularly studies of movement preparation, where established movement-related signatures include the readiness potential (RP), the lateralized readiness potential (LRP), and sensorimotor alpha/beta power decreases and subsequent increases (ERD/ERS) (Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006; Smulders and Miller, 2012; Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017, cf.
text.formatted: Compared with the diverse stimulus-related events, these response events and the processes examined had more direct counterparts in traditional laboratory EEG research, particularly studies of movement preparation, where established movement-related signatures include the readiness potential (RP), the lateralized readiness potential (LRP), and sensorimotor alpha/beta power decreases and subsequent increases (ERD/ERS) <ref type="bibr">(Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Smulders and Miller, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pfurtscheller and</ref> Lopes da Silva, 2017, cf.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
Other studies drew on traditional laboratory EEG research related to action execution and performance monitoring.
Nevertheless, responses differed in the extent to which their timing was freely determined by the player or constrained by ongoing game demands.

In sum, we identified three clusters of response-related analyses: (1) preparation of self-paced actions, (2) action selection and execution during ongoing visuomotor control, and (3) response-related performance monitoring.
(1) Preparation of self-paced actions
One study specifically designed the game Free Wally (Figure 3A) to test whether embedding actions in a meaningful, reason-based context alters neural movement preparation (Verbaarschot et al., 2019).
text.formatted: One study specifically designed the game Free Wally (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>) to test whether embedding actions in a meaningful, reason-based context alters neural movement preparation <ref type="bibr">(Verbaarschot et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Players directed water jets to the left or right to displace approaching agents and protect a captive whale, choosing when and in which direction to act.
A structurally matched control game used visually similar but abstract stimuli without meaningful goals or consequences.
Both conditions elicited an RP beginning approximately 2 s before the response, an LRP emerging approximately 200-400 ms before the response, and sensorimotor alpha/beta ERD followed by ERS.
These patterns did not differ significantly between conditions, suggesting that the meaningful game context did not measurably alter the examined movement-preparation signatures.
An incidental finding in a VR slingshot game extended this evidence (Center et al., 2026).
text.formatted: An incidental finding in a VR slingshot game extended this evidence <ref type="bibr">(Center et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Participants launched balls at color-coded targets by releasing a controller trigger at a freely chosen time.
Ball release was preceded by a slow central negativity beginning approximately 400 ms before the response, consistent with an RP-like buildup.
Release also served as the trigger for the display freezes described in Section 3.3.1.

However, unlike Free Wally, the VR slingshot game used by Center et al. (2026) was designed to investigate disruptions of presence rather than movement preparation, so the preparatory negativity was an additional observation rather than a planned component of interest.
text.formatted: However, unlike Free Wally, the VR slingshot game used by <ref type="bibr">Center et al. (2026)</ref> was designed to investigate disruptions of presence rather than movement preparation, so the preparatory negativity was an additional observation rather than a planned component of interest.

text.text: (2) Action selection and execution during ongoing visuomotor control

Three studies examined response-related activity during ongoing navigation and shooting, where action timing was constrained by approaching obstacles, environment borders, or target availability (Mariman et al., 2023; Anderson et al., 2020; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016).
text.formatted: Three studies examined response-related activity during ongoing navigation and shooting, where action timing was constrained by approaching obstacles, environment borders, or target availability <ref type="bibr">(Mariman et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In a visuomotor game combining cursor navigation and shooting (Figure 3E), beta-band ERD/ERS around both response types changed with practice, most clearly in participants who trained the components separately before combining them in the final session (Mariman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In a visuomotor game combining cursor navigation and shooting (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3E</ref>), beta-band ERD/ERS around both response types changed with practice, most clearly in participants who trained the components separately before combining them in the final session <ref type="bibr">(Mariman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The authors linked these changes to shifting demands on motor control and task integration.
However, navigation movements were shorter on the first day than in the final session, so changes in response duration may also have contributed to the EEG differences.
In the Autoturn variant of Space Fortress, the spaceship automatically aimed at the fortress, while players controlled thrust and firing using separate keys.
Both responses elicited lateralized frontocentral negativities consistent with an LRP (Anderson et al., 2020, cf.
text.formatted: Both responses elicited lateralized frontocentral negativities consistent with an LRP <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2020, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).

Although players chose when to press, thrust responses were constrained by navigation demands, while fortress destruction required 11 shots spaced at least 250 ms apart, followed by one further shot within 250 ms.
Firing too quickly during the initial sequence reset the fortress's accumulated vulnerability.
These movement-preparation signatures thus occurred during actions with substantial spatial and temporal constraints.
Finally, in the space shooter Escape from Asteroid Axon, players navigated a starfighter, collected stars and ammunition, and fired missiles at enemies while avoiding crashes.
Missile launches elicited a frontocentral delta-band negativity around the button press, which the authors interpreted as a correlate of action selection (Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016, Figure 3G).
text.formatted: Missile launches elicited a frontocentral delta-band negativity around the button press, which the authors interpreted as a correlate of action selection <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016</ref>, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3G</ref>).

text.text: (3) Response-related performance monitoring

Two studies examined response-locked potentials resembling the ERN, CRN, and Pe, established laboratory signatures of performance monitoring (Gehring et al., 2012; Vidal et al., 2000; Falkenstein et al., 2000, cf.
text.formatted: Two studies examined response-locked potentials resembling the ERN, CRN, and Pe, established laboratory signatures of performance monitoring <ref type="bibr">(Gehring et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Vidal et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Falkenstein et al., 2000, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1), and related their amplitudes to game performance.
First, Mariman et al. (2023) examined performance monitoring in a visuomotor game combining navigation and shooting.
text.formatted: First, <ref type="bibr">Mariman et al. (2023)</ref> examined performance monitoring in a visuomotor game combining navigation and shooting.

text.text: Participants shot at targets by displacing the right gamepad thumbstick against additional elastic resistance and trained navigation and shooting either together or separately.
EEG activity time-locked to shooting movements showed a positive deflection approximately 200 ms after the end of thumbstick displacement, corresponding to about 600 ms after displacement onset.
The authors interpreted this deflection as Pe-like activity reflecting action monitoring.
Its amplitude decreased with training in the whole-practice group, in parallel with decreasing errors, linking the response-locked activity to improvements in visuomotor performance.

Second, Arake et al. (2022) examined a first-person VR military shooting game in which participants navigated through an environment, took cover, and shot at enemies by pressing the gamepad's "R" button while avoiding being hit.
text.formatted: Second, <ref type="bibr">Arake et al. (2022)</ref> examined a first-person VR military shooting game in which participants navigated through an environment, took cover, and shot at enemies by pressing the gamepad's "R" button while avoiding being hit.

text.text: Gunshots elicited a frontocentral negativity approximately 100 ms after the response, with larger amplitudes following missed than successful shots, which the authors classified as ERN and CRN, respectively.
ERN amplitude also correlated with shooting performance across participants, being larger in those who required fewer shots and less time per kill.
Of note, misses outnumbered hits by about four to one, reversing the ratio of errors to correct responses typically targeted in ERN paradigms (cf. Gehring et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Of note, misses outnumbered hits by about four to one, reversing the ratio of errors to correct responses typically targeted in ERN paradigms (cf. <ref type="bibr">Gehring et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The dominant ERN source was localized to the rostral rather than the more commonly reported dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.

The authors suggested that this localization might reflect negative-affect processing associated with the increased threat of being hit after missing a target, extending the interpretation beyond error detection alone.
Studies appear in text order.
Component identifications follow the original authors' interpretations, with terminology standardized as described in Section 2.5.2 of the main manuscript.
The cognitive processes are those that the study linked to the time-locked response and its neural signature, as reported by its authors.
They are not an independent interpretation by the present review.

In the findings column, latencies, frequency ranges, and electrode sites are given where the original study reported them, at their first mention within an entry. > denotes a larger ERP amplitude for the stated comparison.

ERP, event-related potential.
ERD, event-related desynchronization.
ERS, event-related synchronization.
ACC, anterior cingulate cortex.
CRN, correct-response negativity.
ERN, error-related negativity.
LRP, lateralized readiness potential.
RP, readiness potential.
Pe, error positivity.
VR, virtual reality.
* For Center et al. (2026), only the control condition (standard controller, static non-tracked avatar) is reported here.

text.text: Its embodied, hand-tracked condition lies outside this review's scope.

A majority of the reviewed studies (18 of 29, 62%) reported EEG activity time-locked to feedback-related events, defined as events signaling the rewarding or punishing consequences of players' actions (Table 3).
text.formatted: A majority of the reviewed studies (18 of 29, 62%) reported EEG activity time-locked to feedback-related events, defined as events signaling the rewarding or punishing consequences of players' actions (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Feedback-related events formed the largest event class and the only one examined using commercial titles.

Although these events have apparent counterparts in the outcomes presented in traditional laboratory feedback paradigms, they generally arose from ongoing visuomotor performance and carried consequences for subsequent play.
Notably, the prevalence of feedback-locked analyses did not translate into frequent reports of components specifically associated with feedback processing.
P3-like positivities were the most commonly reported ERP responses, whereas FRN and RewP findings (cf.
Supplementary Material S1) were comparatively rare.
Spectral analyses addressed a broader range of processes, including learning, attention, and affect.

We identified three clusters of feedback-related EEG activity examined in these studies: (1) P3 responses and their sensitivity to outcome properties and player relevance, (2) feedback-and error-related potentials, including the FRN/RewP and anticipatory errorrelated activity, and (3) spectral modulations associated with game outcomes.
(1) Feedback-related P3

P3-like positivities were reported in eight studies, including one reanalysis of an existing dataset, and varied considerably in latency, scalp distribution, and interpretation (Maclin et al., 2011; Mathewson et al., 2012; Anderson et al., 2020 Anderson et al., , 2024;; Fincham et al., 2026; Yokota et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025; Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: P3-like positivities were reported in eight studies, including one reanalysis of an existing dataset, and varied considerably in latency, scalp distribution, and interpretation <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mathewson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several findings resembled the sensitivity of laboratory P3 responses to outcome probability and magnitude (Glazer et al., 2018; Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020, cf.
text.formatted: Several findings resembled the sensitivity of laboratory P3 responses to outcome probability and magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Glazer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020</ref>, cf.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
In two Space Fortress variants, amplitudes were larger for rare deaths than frequent kills (Anderson et al., 2020) and for deaths than missed shots (Anderson et al., 2024, Figure 3F).
text.formatted: In two Space Fortress variants, amplitudes were larger for rare deaths than frequent kills <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2020)</ref> and for deaths than missed shots <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2024, Figure 3F</ref>).

text.text: P3 latency was shortest after kills and longest after vulnerability resets caused by firing too quickly.
The authors attributed this difference to greater predictability of kills and deaths from preceding gameplay, whereas resets occurred more abruptly (Anderson et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The authors attributed this difference to greater predictability of kills and deaths from preceding gameplay, whereas resets occurred more abruptly <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: P3 responses also varied with an outcome's relevance to the individual player.

In a cooperative two-player Space Fortress variant, in which one player drew the fortress's fire while the other attacked it, amplitudes were larger and latencies shorter for a player's own death than for the teammate's, and kill-related amplitudes were larger in the player responsible for the kill (Fincham et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a cooperative two-player Space Fortress variant, in which one player drew the fortress's fire while the other attacked it, amplitudes were larger and latencies shorter for a player's own death than for the teammate's, and kill-related amplitudes were larger in the player responsible for the kill <ref type="bibr">(Fincham et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The authors interpreted this pattern as tracking goal-relevant event boundaries defined by each player's role.

In a two-player baseball game, by contrast, P3 responses did not differ between players, which the authors attributed to similar outcome salience for both, although an earlier frontocentral negativity differed between them (Yokota et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In a two-player baseball game, by contrast, P3 responses did not differ between players, which the authors attributed to similar outcome salience for both, although an earlier frontocentral negativity differed between them <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Three studies explicitly examined relationships between game-related responses and those elicited in laboratory tasks. Maclin et al. (2011) combined Space Fortress with an auditory oddball task before and after training.
text.formatted: Three studies explicitly examined relationships between game-related responses and those elicited in laboratory tasks. <ref type="bibr">Maclin et al. (2011)</ref> combined Space Fortress with an auditory oddball task before and after training.

text.text: The P3 to fortress hits decreased with training while the P3 to oddball tones increased, and both changes correlated with performance improvements.

The authors interpreted this reciprocal pattern as a reallocation of attentional resources freed by automatization of gameplay, consistent with laboratory work on P3 and resource allocation (Isreal et al., 1980; Kramer et al., 1985, cf.
text.formatted: The authors interpreted this reciprocal pattern as a reallocation of attentional resources freed by automatization of gameplay, consistent with laboratory work on P3 and resource allocation <ref type="bibr">(Isreal et al., 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kramer et al., 1985, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
Both responses peaked at approximately 400 ms with a parietal maximum.
By contrast, the P3 to memory-probe mine onsets peaked later, tended to be more frontal, and did not show this reciprocity (Section 3.3.1).

Pei et al. (2025) examined a custom-built reimplementation of Flappy Bird, a side-scrolling game in which players repeatedly tap to keep a bird airborne and guide it through gaps between pipes that act as obstacles.
They compared EEG responses to the bird colliding with a pipe with ERPs from five laboratory tasks recorded in a separate cohort.
Collisions elicited a broadly distributed central positivity around 300 ms that exceeded the laboratory responses and increased rather than habituated across the initial blocks.
Although resembling the classic P3, particularly the novelty P3 (Polich, 2007; Ranganath and Rainer, 2003, cf.
text.formatted: Although resembling the classic P3, particularly the novelty P3 <ref type="bibr">(Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ranganath and Rainer, 2003, cf</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1), its amplitude and persistence led the authors to propose a distinct critical-event variant, the P300-CE.
They characterized it as endogenous because collisions involved no abrupt visual change.
Finally, Cavanagh and Castellanos (2016) trained classifiers on EEG from oddball and gambling tasks completed by the same participants before gameplay.

Rewarding missile hits and punishing crashes in Escape from Asteroid Axon both showed a bias toward oddball-target patterns within the canonical P3 time range, suggesting shared salience-detection processes.
Missile hits additionally resembled gambling wins, whereas crashes were not classified as losses and leaned slightly toward wins.
Unlike gambling losses, crashes lacked strong frontal midline theta and showed a shorter ERP time course.
The authors suggested that crashes may not have elicited the same need for cognitive control, or that gambling losses capture only one way of processing unfavorable outcomes.

(2) Feedback-and error-related potentials Only one of the reviewed studies explicitly distinguished both an FRN and a RewP, reporting these components following misses and hits, respectively, in a VR game in which players shot down approaching cannonballs (Yokota and Naruse, 2021, Figure 3H).
text.formatted: (2) Feedback-and error-related potentials Only one of the reviewed studies explicitly distinguished both an FRN and a RewP, reporting these components following misses and hits, respectively, in a VR game in which players shot down approaching cannonballs (Yokota and Naruse, 2021, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3H</ref>).

text.text: Cannonball curvature and size varied task difficulty and thus the assumed probability of a hit, while time pressure and accumulated damage varied the consequences of the outcome.
The FRN was larger in easier situations, when misses were unexpected.
The RewP was larger in harder situations, when hits were unexpected, and when outcomes were more consequential.
These effects broadly corresponded to laboratory findings on outcome probability and magnitude (Sambrook and Goslin, 2015; Paul et al., 2020 Paul et al., , 2025, cf, cf.

text.text: Supplementary Material S1).
Several studies reported deflections in the same latency range as the FRN and RewP with tentative or no component identification.

In cooperative Space Fortress, Anderson et al. (2024) identified a frontocentral negativity within a principal component separating punishing from rewarding outcomes and suggested a correspondence to the FRN.
text.formatted: In cooperative Space Fortress, <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al. (2024)</ref> identified a frontocentral negativity within a principal component separating punishing from rewarding outcomes and suggested a correspondence to the FRN.

text.text: In Escape from Asteroid Axon, Cavanagh and Castellanos (2016) tentatively associated the plateau following the P2 to missile hits with the RewP.

Other studies reported positivities after rewarding collections in a spacenavigation game (Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021) or negativities after kills and vulnerability resets in Space Fortress (Anderson et al., 2020), without assigning them to specific components.

text.text: Three studies reported negativities shortly before or at the onset of punishing outcomes (Yokota et al., 2019; Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021; Spüler and Niethammer, 2015).

text.text: (3) Spectral modulations associated with game outcomes
Feedback-related spectral analyses most often examined alpha power or hemispheric alpha asymmetries, followed by theta and delta power, with beta and gamma modulations reported less frequently.
Correspondence with laboratory associations between outcome valence and oscillatory activity was mixed.
Laboratory studies commonly report increased frontal midline theta after unfavorable outcomes and increased delta or frontal beta after favorable outcomes (Luft, 2014; Glazer et al., 2018, cf.

In the reviewed games, delta and beta increases occurred after both rewarding and punishing events (Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Li et al., 2025; Salminen and Ravaja, 2007).

text.text: Other studies emphasized attention, arousal, and motor demands.
In Super Monkey Ball 2, players tilted a platform to guide a ball-encased monkey toward a goal while collecting tokens and avoiding falls.
Token collection, often requiring risky steering near platform edges, was followed by reduced frontal high-alpha power, interpreted as increased attention.
Goal completion elicited increased parietal theta and widespread alpha power, interpreted as relaxation after reaching the goal (Salminen and Ravaja, 2007).
