text.text: Abbreviations: EEG, electroencephalography.
ERP, event-related potential.
ERD, event-related desynchronization.
ERS, event-related synchronization.
ERSP, event-related spectral perturbation.
ERN, error-related negativity.
FRN, feedback-related negativity.
RewP, reward positivity.
Pe, error positivity.
PCA, principal component analysis.
MOBA, multiplayer online battle arena.
VR, virtual reality.
This scoping review mapped how video game paradigms have been used to examine eventrelated EEG activity during gameplay.

The findings indicate that established neural signatures can be observed during ongoing, goal-directed behavior, although their correspondence with laboratory effects varies across components and paradigms.
This highlights the potential of video games to extend cognitive EEG research while raising questions about how gameplay shapes the measurement and interpretation of neural responses.
In the following, we first summarize the current use of video games as event-related EEG paradigms in the reviewed literature (Section 4.1).
We then discuss converging and diverging findings on event-related EEG effects between the video game studies reviewed here and conventional laboratory paradigms (Section 4.2).
In Section 4.3, we address recurring methodological challenges associated with using video game paradigms for event-related EEG research and how these challenges may be addressed.
Finally, after acknowledging some limitations of the current scoping review, we close with potential directions for future research at the intersection of video game paradigms and EEG research.
The reviewed literature used a diverse set of video game paradigms, although most were custom-built and involved navigation and/or targeting during continuous gameplay.
Across 29 studies, we identified 26 distinct paradigms, of which 19 were custom-built, 20 involved navigation and/or targeting, and 20 lacked bounded decision or action epochs.

Repeated use across studies was concentrated in Space Fortress (Donchin, 1989), represented by three variants across five studies (Maclin et al., 2011; Mathewson et al., 2012; Anderson et al., 2020 Anderson et al., , 2024;; Fincham et al., 2026), and a VR go/no-go multitasking game examined in two studies (Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026).
text.formatted: Repeated use across studies was concentrated in Space Fortress <ref type="bibr">(Donchin, 1989)</ref>, represented by three variants across five studies <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mathewson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026)</ref>, and a VR go/no-go multitasking game examined in two studies <ref type="bibr">(Sanuki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiao and Iramina, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The reviewed studies illustrate how tasks and manipulations from traditional laboratory research can be embedded in gameplay.

Examples include go/no-go contingencies to probe cognitive control (Petras et al., 2016; Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026), self-paced voluntary responses to study deliberate action (Verbaarschot et al., 2019), operationalizations of outcome probability and magnitude through task geometry and game progress (Yokota and Naruse, 2021), and volatile reinforcement structures to examine probabilistic decision-making (Eguinoa et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Examples include go/no-go contingencies to probe cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sanuki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiao and Iramina, 2026)</ref>, self-paced voluntary responses to study deliberate action <ref type="bibr">(Verbaarschot et al., 2019)</ref>, operationalizations of outcome probability and magnitude through task geometry and game progress <ref type="bibr">(Yokota and Naruse, 2021)</ref>, and volatile reinforcement structures to examine probabilistic decision-making <ref type="bibr">(Eguinoa et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Gameplay also provides ways to establish an event's relevance through the player's goals and role.
In a taxi-driving game, the same stores served as targets or nontargets depending on the passenger's destination (Weidemann et al., 2009).
text.formatted: In a taxi-driving game, the same stores served as targets or nontargets depending on the passenger's destination <ref type="bibr">(Weidemann et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: In two-player games, events on a shared display elicited different neural responses depending on the player's role (Yokota et al., 2019; Fincham et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In two-player games, events on a shared display elicited different neural responses depending on the player's role <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In Flappy Bird, collisions were analyzed as changes in the game situation without an abrupt visual change at the event itself (Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In Flappy Bird, collisions were analyzed as changes in the game situation without an abrupt visual change at the event itself <ref type="bibr">(Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These examples illustrate how video game paradigms can incorporate traditional laboratory tasks while also making event relevance depend on the unfolding context of play.

They provide opportunities to examine goal-related significance beyond differences in the physical stimulus, although the extent to which these influences can be separated depends on the individual design.
The events selected for EEG analysis were unevenly distributed across these paradigms.
Feedback-locked analyses were used in 16 of the 26 paradigms, stimulus-locked analyses in nine, and response-locked analyses in only six.
Only three studies made movement preparation, motor learning, or response-locked error processing a primary objective (Verbaarschot et al., 2019; Mariman et al., 2023; Arake et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Only three studies made movement preparation, motor learning, or response-locked error processing a primary objective <ref type="bibr">(Verbaarschot et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mariman et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Arake et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This distribution may partly reflect the predominance of continuous gameplay.
Objects often approach gradually, and navigation may require sustained control, while hits, collisions, and deaths provide discrete events for time-locking.
Access to event timing may also contribute.
Studies using commercial titles relied on external event annotation, for instance from screen recordings, and all included feedback-locked analyses.
Because most commercial paradigms also involved continuous gameplay, the contributions of game structure and event access cannot be separated from this review.

Nevertheless, gradual stimulus changes and extended actions can support event-related analyses when events are defined operationally, as illustrated by the display size of an approached object (Weidemann et al., 2009) and the onset and offset of thumbstick displacement (Mariman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, gradual stimulus changes and extended actions can support event-related analyses when events are defined operationally, as illustrated by the display size of an approached object <ref type="bibr">(Weidemann et al., 2009)</ref> and the onset and offset of thumbstick displacement <ref type="bibr">(Mariman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The current distribution of analyses may therefore reflect both researchers' objectives and the events that their selected games make accessible.

In the following, we discuss points of convergence and divergence between the event-related EEG effects observed using video game paradigms and more traditional laboratory paradigms, broadly ordered by their frequency of observation in the reviewed literature.
Throughout, we distinguish similarities in response morphology and functional sensitivity from evidence provided by direct comparisons with laboratory tasks.
P3-like positivities provided the most frequently reported evidence of convergence between video game paradigms and traditional laboratory tasks.

They occurred across event types, including go/no-go stimuli (Petras et al., 2016; Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026), memory probe-like mine onsets (Maclin et al., 2011), display freezes (Center et al., 2026), and rewarding and punishing outcomes (Maclin et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2020 Anderson et al., , 2024;; Fincham et al., 2026; Yokota et al., 2019; Li et al., 2025; Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: They occurred across event types, including go/no-go stimuli <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sanuki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiao and Iramina, 2026)</ref>, memory probe-like mine onsets <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011)</ref>, display freezes <ref type="bibr">(Center et al., 2026)</ref>, and rewarding and punishing outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond their resemblance in latency and scalp distribution, several responses varied with factors known to modulate the laboratory P3.

Outcome-related amplitudes varied with event probability (Anderson et al., 2020) and outcome magnitude (Anderson et al., 2024), consistent with laboratory findings on expectancy and magnitude (Hajcak et al., 2005; Glazer et al., 2018; Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020; Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Outcome-related amplitudes varied with event probability <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2020)</ref> and outcome magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2024)</ref>, consistent with laboratory findings on expectancy and magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Hajcak et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Glazer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: P3 latency also varied with the predictability of outcomes from preceding gameplay (Anderson et al., 2020), while both amplitude and latency depended on an event's relevance to the individual player (Fincham et al., 2026 , cf. Yokota et al., 2019).

Yokota et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that P3-like responses during gameplay retain sensitivity to event probability, magnitude, and relevance, although these similarities alone do not establish that the underlying processes are identical.
Studies that compared game-elicited positivities with laboratory responses more directly revealed both similarities and differences.
The P3 to rewarding fortress hits showed a reciprocal relationship with the P3 to tones in a concurrent oddball task, consistent with shared attentional resources (Maclin et al., 2011).
text.formatted: The P3 to rewarding fortress hits showed a reciprocal relationship with the P3 to tones in a concurrent oddball task, consistent with shared attentional resources <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Rewarding and punishing outcomes in Escape from Asteroid Axon also resembled oddball targets in cross-paradigm classification (Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016).
text.formatted: Rewarding and punishing outcomes in Escape from Asteroid Axon also resembled oddball targets in cross-paradigm classification <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, pipe collisions in Flappy Bird elicited a positivity that was larger and more persistent across repetitions than responses in traditional laboratory tasks, including a reinforcementlearning task, leading the authors to propose the P300-CE (Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In contrast, pipe collisions in Flappy Bird elicited a positivity that was larger and more persistent across repetitions than responses in traditional laboratory tasks, including a reinforcementlearning task, leading the authors to propose the P300-CE <ref type="bibr">(Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest convergence in resource allocation and spatiotemporal response patterns alongside differences in amplitude and habituation.
Because the studies tested different properties, they do not establish a uniform correspondence or a general divergence between game-elicited and laboratory P3 responses.

Several authors interpreted the game-elicited positivities primarily in terms of the salience and goal relevance of critical game events (Anderson et al., 2020 (Anderson et al., , 2024;; Fincham et al., 2026; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Pei et al., 2025) or the attentional resources they engage (Maclin et al., 2011; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Fincham et al., 2026; Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Several authors interpreted the game-elicited positivities primarily in terms of the salience and goal relevance of critical game events <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pei et al., 2025)</ref> or the attentional resources they engage <ref type="bibr">(Maclin et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This emphasis is compatible with traditional laboratory accounts of the P3 that stress behavioral relevance and motivational significance (Walentowska et al., 2016), but leaves less direct evidence about whether these responses track outcome valence, reward prediction errors, or learning during gameplay.
text.formatted: This emphasis is compatible with traditional laboratory accounts of the P3 that stress behavioral relevance and motivational significance <ref type="bibr">(Walentowska et al., 2016)</ref>, but leaves less direct evidence about whether these responses track outcome valence, reward prediction errors, or learning during gameplay.

text.text: Evidence for convergence with traditional laboratory measures of error and feedback processing was more limited.
Although feedback-locked analyses were reported in 18 of the 29 studies, only four related their findings to the FRN or RewP.

One study specifically delineated both components (Yokota and Naruse, 2021), two proposed these correspondences tentatively (Anderson et al., 2024; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016), and one examined perturbations of ongoing control rather than action outcomes (Spüler and Niethammer, 2015).
text.formatted: One study specifically delineated both components <ref type="bibr">(Yokota and Naruse, 2021)</ref>, two proposed these correspondences tentatively <ref type="bibr">(Anderson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016)</ref>, and one examined perturbations of ongoing control rather than action outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Spüler and Niethammer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Reports of ERN-, CRN-, or Pe-like activity were also uncommon and extended beyond the response events to which these components are conventionally time-locked.

Of the six events associated with such activity, two were responses (Arake et al., 2022; Mariman et al., 2023), two were perturbations of ongoing control (Spüler and Niethammer, 2015; Wimmer et al., 2024), and two were punishing outcomes (Yokota et al., 2019; Spüler and Niethammer, 2015).
text.formatted: Of the six events associated with such activity, two were responses <ref type="bibr">(Arake et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mariman et al., 2023)</ref>, two were perturbations of ongoing control <ref type="bibr">(Spüler and Niethammer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wimmer et al., 2024)</ref>, and two were punishing outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Spüler and Niethammer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern limits conclusions about correspondence with laboratory components, but does not establish their absence during gameplay.

It also raises the question of whether conventional distinctions between response-related errors and externally presented feedback adequately describe performance monitoring during continuous game control.
The motor-control literature offers a useful framework for interpreting this pattern.
Most reviewed paradigms required navigation and/or targeting (20 of 26), making the precision and timing of ongoing movements central to performance.

Such demands resemble tracking, aiming, and throwing tasks, whereas traditional laboratory studies of the ERN and FRN have often used discrete choices and outcomes in speeded-response, gambling, time-estimation, and learning tasks (Gehring et al., 2012; Sambrook and Goslin, 2015; Faßbender et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such demands resemble tracking, aiming, and throwing tasks, whereas traditional laboratory studies of the ERN and FRN have often used discrete choices and outcomes in speeded-response, gambling, time-estimation, and learning tasks <ref type="bibr">(Gehring et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sambrook and Goslin, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Faßbender et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: During continuous control, errors can arise from action selection, movement execution, or failure to achieve the task goal (Krigolson and Holroyd, 2006, 2007a).
text.formatted: During continuous control, errors can arise from action selection, movement execution, or failure to achieve the task goal <ref type="bibr">(Krigolson and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holroyd, 2006, 2007a)</ref>.

text.text: Information about performance accumulates through efferent, proprioceptive, and visual signals, so an impending miss or collision may be apparent before the game registers the outcome.

Consequently, a single erroneous response may be difficult to identify, and the internal and external information conventionally associated with the ERN and FRN may overlap (Krigolson, 2018; Maurer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Consequently, a single erroneous response may be difficult to identify, and the internal and external information conventionally associated with the ERN and FRN may overlap <ref type="bibr">(Krigolson, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maurer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: One proposed distinction separates movement errors, or deviations from intended movement parameters, from action-effect errors, or failures to achieve the action goal.

For action-effect errors, this account distinguishes predictive error valuation before feedback from postdictive valuation after feedback, associating these with the ERN and FRN, respectively (Maurer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For action-effect errors, this account distinguishes predictive error valuation before feedback from postdictive valuation after feedback, associating these with the ERN and FRN, respectively <ref type="bibr">(Maurer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This framework offers a possible interpretation of negativities preceding punishing game outcomes (Yokota et al., 2019; Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021; Spüler and Niethammer, 2015), which may resemble responses to predictable errors in tracking and throwing tasks (Krigolson and Holroyd, 2007b; Maurer et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This framework offers a possible interpretation of negativities preceding punishing game outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Spüler and Niethammer, 2015)</ref>, which may resemble responses to predictable errors in tracking and throwing tasks <ref type="bibr">(Krigolson and Holroyd, 2007b;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Maurer et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Likewise, activity time-locked to game-induced perturbations can be related to motor-control studies that introduce unexpected deviations during ongoing movement (Krigolson and Holroyd, 2006, 2007a; Krigolson et al., 2008; Anguera et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Likewise, activity time-locked to game-induced perturbations can be related to motor-control studies that introduce unexpected deviations during ongoing movement <ref type="bibr">(Krigolson and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holroyd, 2006, 2007a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krigolson et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anguera et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Motor-control findings also identify two sources of variability relevant to gameplay: error-related activity scales with graded error magnitude (Anguera et al., 2009; Frömer et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2022), and learning can shift error valuation toward prediction, with increasing ERN and decreasing FRN amplitudes (Maurer et al., 2022).

text.text: Differences in error magnitude and stage of practice may therefore contribute to variation across game studies, even when events share the same label.
The context and consequences of game outcomes offer another possible explanation for differences from traditional laboratory findings.
Feedback-locked activity can reflect overlapping contributions from reward prediction errors, surprise, and salience (Ullsperger, 2024), whose relative contributions may differ across tasks.
During gameplay, an outcome may be predictable from the preceding action yet remain consequential because it changes the player's situation or prospects for subsequent play.
A missed shot, for example, may leave the player exposed to attack.

Such consequences could alter attentional and affective responses beyond those elicited by an abstract gain or loss, although the reviewed studies did not isolate this influence from differences in task structure.

This possibility is consistent with the larger and more persistent positivity following collisions in Flappy Bird (Pei et al., 2025) and with the finding that crashes in Escape from Asteroid Axon did not resemble gambling losses in cross-paradigm classification (Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016).

text.text: These findings suggest that describing events as "errors"
or "negative feedback" is insufficient to establish their functional equivalence across game and laboratory paradigms.
Whether differences arise from continuous control, the consequences of outcomes, or their combination remains unresolved.
Movement-related findings provided more direct evidence of convergence, although only a few studies examined them.

In the clearest controlled comparison, the RP, LRP, and sensorimotor ERD/ERS associated with deliberate actions did not differ significantly between a meaningful game and a structurally matched control game with visually similar but abstract stimuli (Verbaarschot et al., 2019).

Both this paradigm and a VR slingshot game permitted self-paced responses and elicited an RP (Center et al., 2026).

text.text: The available evidence therefore supports the occurrence of established movement-related signatures during gameplay, while highlighting the need to distinguish effects of game context from differences in response timing and movement execution.
For early sensory components, the evidence was too sparse to assess convergence with traditional laboratory findings.
Only isolated studies reported P1 or N1 effects (Petras et al., 2016; Wimmer et al., 2024).

text.text: Their limited coverage may reflect the reviewed studies' emphasis on later components, as well as difficulties in isolating early sensory responses during gameplay.
Early visual components are sensitive to luminance, contrast, and other physical stimulus properties (Luck, 2014), which may vary continuously within a game.

text.text: These constraints offer possible explanations for the limited evidence, but do not demonstrate that early sensory components are absent or fundamentally different during gameplay.
The review therefore provides a stronger basis for evaluating later, endogenous responses than early sensory processing.
Spectral findings showed selective correspondences with traditional laboratory findings, but substantial differences in tasks and analyses limited comparisons across studies.

Theta modulations, mostly at frontal sites, distinguished successful from failed go responses (Sanuki et al., 2022), increased with training in proportion to performance gains (Qiao and Iramina, 2026), differed between goal-relevant and irrelevant objects (Weidemann et al., 2009), and scaled with trial-wise prediction errors (Eguinoa et al., 2026).

text.text: Feedbackrelated spectral activity corresponded less consistently to laboratory associations with outcome valence.

Delta and beta power increased after both rewarding and punishing events, while the frontal midline theta enhancement often associated with unfavorable outcomes was not consistently observed (Salminen and Ravaja, 2007; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016).

text.text: Delta increases also coincided or covaried with P3 responses to the same events (Maclin et al., 2011; Li et al., 2025), leaving open whether they provided distinct evidence about outcome processing.

text.text: Other alpha and beta effects were interpreted in terms of attention, arousal, or workload (Salminen and Ravaja, 2007; Chang et al., 2022; Bernal et al., 2024), but sensory-modality differences (Chang et al., 2022), unreported event rarity (Bernal et al., 2024), and concurrent motor activity (Salminen and Ravaja, 2007) limited the specificity of these interpretations.

text.text: Some asymmetry measures covered intervals of several seconds, providing only coarse temporal information about outcome processing (Shin et al., 2012; Rebert et al., 1984).

text.text: The spectral evidence therefore supports some functional parallels with laboratory findings, but rarely isolates whether a modulation reflects outcome evaluation, sensory processing, or the motor demands accompanying the event.

Four recurring methodological challenges emerged across the reviewed studies: establishing precise event markers, controlling low-level stimulus properties, separating temporally adjacent events, and accounting for event probabilities and outcome magnitude.
The following discussion considers how these challenges affect the interpretation of event-related EEG during gameplay and, with examples from the reviewed studies, how they may be addressed.
Precise event marking requires distinguishing when an event occurs in the game engine, when it becomes perceptually available, and when it is recorded relative to the EEG.
Access to these timestamps depends partly on the choice of game.
Studies using commercial titles marked events manually during gameplay (Shin et al., 2012) or retrospectively from video frames (Yokota et al., 2019; Salminen and Ravaja, 2008; Li et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Studies using commercial titles marked events manually during gameplay <ref type="bibr">(Shin et al., 2012)</ref> or retrospectively from video frames <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Salminen and Ravaja, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Li et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Frame-based annotation can identify visible changes, but its precision depends on recording frame rate, synchronization with the EEG, and the consistency of event identification. Li et al. (2025) addressed several of these issues by using two independent raters, correcting for a measured screen-mirroring delay, quantifying inter-rater consistency, and releasing gameplay recordings and the annotation protocol.
text.formatted: Frame-based annotation can identify visible changes, but its precision depends on recording frame rate, synchronization with the EEG, and the consistency of event identification. <ref type="bibr">Li et al. (2025)</ref> addressed several of these issues by using two independent raters, correcting for a measured screen-mirroring delay, quantifying inter-rater consistency, and releasing gameplay recordings and the annotation protocol.

text.text: Custom-built games facilitate direct event logging, but engine timestamps still require validation against the actual presentation of stimuli, including display delays and refresh timing.

Recording both actions and their outcomes is particularly valuable when interpreting activity that precedes an outcome, because its timing relative to the preceding movement may distinguish preparatory activity from outcome anticipation.

Events that emerge gradually require an explicit operational definition in addition to an accurate timestamp. Weidemann et al. (2009), for example, defined onset by the display size at which an object was reliably being approached.
text.formatted: Events that emerge gradually require an explicit operational definition in addition to an accurate timestamp. <ref type="bibr">Weidemann et al. (2009)</ref>, for example, defined onset by the display size at which an object was reliably being approached.

text.text: This provides a reproducible marker, but it need not coincide with perceptual detection, categorization, or response initiation.
Event-marking procedures should therefore report both their temporal uncertainty and the stage of the unfolding event that the marker represents.
Precise event timing alone does not establish what an event-related response reflects.
Attributing an ERP difference to an event's psychological significance also requires accounting for differences in its physical properties.

Luminance, contrast, size, and sensory modality can influence ERP responses independently of the cognitive process under investigation, particularly at early sensory latencies but also at later stages (Luck, 2014).
text.formatted: Luminance, contrast, size, and sensory modality can influence ERP responses independently of the cognitive process under investigation, particularly at early sensory latencies but also at later stages <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Luck, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In video games, these properties may vary systematically between event classes because events occur within changing scenes and their appearance is tied to gameplay.

Go and no-go stimuli may differ visually (Petras et al., 2016), while player perspective and presentation modality may introduce differences in target size, visual complexity, or cross-modal predictability (Petras et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Go and no-go stimuli may differ visually <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016)</ref>, while player perspective and presentation modality may introduce differences in target size, visual complexity, or cross-modal predictability <ref type="bibr">(Petras et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: An event that interrupts gameplay may also elicit a response to the accompanying visual interruption. Spüler and Niethammer (2015) addressed this problem by delaying the game pause until one second after a collision.
text.formatted: An event that interrupts gameplay may also elicit a response to the accompanying visual interruption. <ref type="bibr">Spüler and Niethammer (2015)</ref> addressed this problem by delaying the game pause until one second after a collision.

text.text: These examples illustrate the need to distinguish the event of interest from sensory changes that accompany it.
Where possible, stimulus properties should be matched across conditions or varied independently of the psychological contrast.
Gameplay can support this separation by assigning different significance to the same stimulus through changes in the player's goals or role, as illustrated in Section 4.1.
Even when physical differences between event classes are controlled, the response elicited by each class may combine sensory and cognitive activity.

Two studies argued against a purely visual explanation because the event involved no abrupt change in visual input (Pei et al., 2025) or did not stand out from the visually rich gameplay surrounding it (Salminen and Ravaja, 2008).
text.formatted: Two studies argued against a purely visual explanation because the event involved no abrupt change in visual input <ref type="bibr">(Pei et al., 2025)</ref> or did not stand out from the visually rich gameplay surrounding it <ref type="bibr">(Salminen and Ravaja, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These observations help characterize the eliciting event, but do not by themselves isolate the processing of its meaning.
Conversely, visual effects such as a screen flash when the player is hit can introduce a sensory response that coincides with outcome processing (Shin et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Conversely, visual effects such as a screen flash when the player is hit can introduce a sensory response that coincides with outcome processing <ref type="bibr">(Shin et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Interpreting event-locked activity therefore requires documenting the sensory changes accompanying an event and, where feasible, using matched control conditions to distinguish their contribution from that of the event's task relevance.
A further challenge is separating the response to an event from activity elicited by neighboring events.
Closely spaced game events can produce overlapping EEG responses, making activity attributed to one event partly reflect preceding or subsequent events.

This problem is especially relevant when actions and outcomes follow one another rapidly or when collectibles are placed near hazards, allowing rewarding and punishing events to occur in close succession.
Increasing event spacing can reduce overlap, but may also alter the gameplay under investigation.

Several reviewed studies incorporated temporal separation into the game mechanics: stimuli appeared at controlled intervals during otherwise continuous play (Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026; Maclin et al., 2011), recharge delays or shot-spacing rules shaped the timing of actions (Arake et al., 2022; Maclin et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2020), and bounded action epochs introduced a trial-like structure (Verbaarschot et al., 2019; Petras et al., 2016; Center et al., 2026; Eguinoa et al., 2026).

text.text: Such constraints should be evaluated against the time course of the responses of interest, since a minimum interval between actions does not necessarily prevent their neural responses from overlapping.

Other studies excluded overlapping epochs (Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021; Arake et al., 2022; Mariman et al., 2023; Li et al., 2025) or retained only the first event within a specified window (Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016).

text.text: These approaches reduce the available data and may preferentially retain periods of less eventful gameplay.

Where temporal separation would undermine the intended task, deconvolution methods offer an alternative for estimating overlapping responses, provided that the relevant events are recorded and the design supports their separation (Ehinger and Dimigen, 2019).
text.formatted: Where temporal separation would undermine the intended task, deconvolution methods offer an alternative for estimating overlapping responses, provided that the relevant events are recorded and the design supports their separation <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ehinger and Dimigen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Event probability and outcome magnitude also influence many canonical EEG components.
In video games, these quantities may depend on the unfolding situation and the player's skill rather than on an experimentally fixed schedule (e.g., Arake et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In video games, these quantities may depend on the unfolding situation and the player's skill rather than on an experimentally fixed schedule (e.g., <ref type="bibr">Arake et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Differences attributed to event type or outcome valence may therefore also reflect differences in rarity, predictability, vestigation where the task permits, with interval distributions reported and overlap correction considered when temporal separation is impractical (Ehinger and Dimigen, 2019).
text.formatted: Differences attributed to event type or outcome valence may therefore also reflect differences in rarity, predictability, vestigation where the task permits, with interval distributions reported and overlap correction considered when temporal separation is impractical <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ehinger and Dimigen, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: For continuously controlled games, design and analysis should additionally account for graded movement errors and outcomes, drawing on the motor-control ERP literature rather than relying exclusively on categories developed for discrete choices.

Finally, functional interpretations should be supported by evidence beyond response morphology, for example by relating single-trial activity to model-derived quantities (Eguinoa et al., 2026), component amplitudes to behavioral performance (Arake et al., 2022), or neural measures to performance on independently administered tasks (Mathewson et al., 2012), and by comparing game-elicited responses with those from matched control or laboratory tasks (Verbaarschot et al., 2019; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Finally, functional interpretations should be supported by evidence beyond response morphology, for example by relating single-trial activity to model-derived quantities <ref type="bibr">(Eguinoa et al., 2026)</ref>, component amplitudes to behavioral performance <ref type="bibr">(Arake et al., 2022)</ref>, or neural measures to performance on independently administered tasks <ref type="bibr">(Mathewson et al., 2012)</ref>, and by comparing game-elicited responses with those from matched control or laboratory tasks <ref type="bibr">(Verbaarschot et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several limitations of the present review should be acknowledged.
First, our search strategy may have missed eligible studies that did not describe their paradigms using terms such as "video game," "computer game," or "VR game."

Our exclusion of studies focusing primarily on emotion or multi-feature classification may have omitted relevant individual findings, and the exclusion of BCI-related titles may have eliminated studies that use BCI terminology to describe their EEG systems or applicability of their findings without having actually used neural input for game control.
We attempted to mitigate the latter through careful screening at the abstract and full-text stages, which led to the inclusion of two studies despite BCI-related terminology.
The wider BCI literature, which frequently employs game-like environments, may nevertheless contain further findings relevant to cognitive event-related EEG research that our criteria excluded.
Second, determining whether a paradigm qualifies as a video game is inherently difficult, given the broad range of possible definitions (Arjoranta, 2019; Stenros, 2017).
text.formatted: Second, determining whether a paradigm qualifies as a video game is inherently difficult, given the broad range of possible definitions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Arjoranta, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Stenros, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Our operational definition, based on that proposed by Allen et al. (2024), emphasized intuitive interaction and engagement as the features most relevant for advancing ecological validity in psychological research, but alternative criteria could lead to different inclusion decisions.

Third, as is appropriate for a scoping review, we did not conduct a formal quality assessment of the included studies or systematically evaluate whether their analysis methods aligned with current standards.
The synthesis should therefore not be read as implying that the included studies provide equally strong evidence.

Moreover, to relate the findings to the extensive existing literature, our categorization of events and components relied on conventional definitions and time-locking conventions, for example response-locked measurement for the ERN.
In several cases, this categorization diverged from the authors' original interpretations and may not fully capture the range of neural signatures the authors intended to highlight.
As argued in Section 4.2, this taxonomy is itself of limited applicability to continuously controlled paradigms.
The organization of our findings is therefore best understood as a framework for relating game-elicited activity to canonical paradigms and effects.
Finally, most of the patterns reported here rest on few and unevenly distributed studies, often on a single one, and should be read as descriptive observations rather than as tested claims.
Potential future research The current state of event-related EEG research with video games suggests several potential directions for further investigation.

Building on the methodological challenges and recommendations discussed in Section 4.3, future work could examine how gameplay affects the measurement and interpretation of neural responses, consolidate findings that currently rest on few studies, and explore neurocognitive questions that have received limited attention in the video game EEG literature to date.
We consider these possibilities in turn.
One potential direction concerns the role of temporal structure in relating game-elicited responses to established laboratory effects.
Several studies reported close correspondences in games organized into bounded, trial-like epochs (Verbaarschot et al., 2019; Yokota and Naruse, 2021; Eguinoa et al., 2026).

text.text: Others embedded discrete events within continuous gameplay using controlled stimulus intervals or shot-timing rules (Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026; Maclin et al., 2011; Anderson et al., 2020; Arake et al., 2022).

text.text: These findings leave open how much temporal separation is needed to identify the responses of interest and how imposing such separation changes gameplay.

Comparisons of different temporal arrangements could help clarify when event spacing is beneficial and when analytical approaches to overlapping responses might offer a suitable alternative (Ehinger and Dimigen, 2019).

text.text: Another direction concerns the criteria used to identify and interpret game-elicited responses.

Where responses differ from their laboratory counterparts, it remains unclear when they should retain an established component label and when a new label might be warranted, as proposed for the P300-CE (Pei et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Where responses differ from their laboratory counterparts, it remains unclear when they should retain an established component label and when a new label might be warranted, as proposed for the P300-CE <ref type="bibr">(Pei et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Further work could examine how morphological similarities are supported by direct comparisons with matched control or laboratory tasks (Verbaarschot et al., 2019; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Pei et al., 2025), relationships with model-derived quantities (Eguinoa et al., 2026), behavioral performance (Arake et al., 2022), or performance on independently administered tasks (Mathewson et al., 2012).

text.text: For continuous gameplay, it may also be useful to examine whether conventional distinctions between stimuli, responses, errors, and feedback adequately describe the unfolding activity, drawing on distinctions developed in motor-control research (Maurer et al., 2021).

text.text: Many findings in the reviewed literature rest on individual studies, leaving their reproducibility and generalizability across games uncertain.
Replication within the same paradigm and comparisons across games could help establish which response properties persist across implementations.

For P3-like positivities, this includes both the reported sensitivities to event probability, magnitude, and player relevance (Anderson et al., 2020 (Anderson et al., , 2024;; Fincham et al., 2026) and the similarities and differences observed in comparisons with laboratory responses (Maclin et al., 2011; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016; Pei et al., 2025).

text.text: Further matched comparisons could likewise establish how broadly the preservation of movement-preparation signatures observed in Free Wally extends to other games and action demands (Verbaarschot et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Further matched comparisons could likewise establish how broadly the preservation of movement-preparation signatures observed in Free Wally extends to other games and action demands <ref type="bibr">(Verbaarschot et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Targeted studies could also clarify findings that were infrequent or identified only tentatively.

These include FRN-and RewP-like responses to game outcomes (Yokota and Naruse, 2021; Anderson et al., 2024; Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016) and error-related activity during responses, perturbations, and punishing outcomes (Arake et al., 2022; Mariman et al., 2023; Spüler and Niethammer, 2015; Wimmer et al., 2024; Yokota et al., 2019).
text.formatted: These include FRN-and RewP-like responses to game outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Yokota and Naruse, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Anderson et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh and Castellanos, 2016)</ref> and error-related activity during responses, perturbations, and punishing outcomes <ref type="bibr">(Arake et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Mariman et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Spüler and Niethammer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Wimmer et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">Yokota et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Examining these responses under comparable task conditions could help distinguish inconsistent effects from differences in event definition, gameplay demands, or the studies' original objectives.
The same consideration applies to spectral findings, for which similarities in frequency band do not necessarily imply similarities in function.

Replicating reported relationships with performance, learning, or prediction errors could provide firmer evidence about which functional associations generalize across game paradigms (Sanuki et al., 2022; Qiao and Iramina, 2026; Eguinoa et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Replicating reported relationships with performance, learning, or prediction errors could provide firmer evidence about which functional associations generalize across game paradigms <ref type="bibr">(Sanuki et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Qiao and Iramina, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eguinoa et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Continuous gameplay may provide opportunities to examine how performance monitoring unfolds across an action rather than only at a discrete response or outcome.

Negativities preceding punishing outcomes suggest that relevant information can become available before the game registers failure (Yokota et al., 2019; Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021; Spüler and Niethammer, 2015).
text.formatted: Negativities preceding punishing outcomes suggest that relevant information can become available before the game registers failure <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Martínez-Tejada et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Spüler and Niethammer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Building on motor-control research (Maurer et al., 2021 (Maurer et al., , 2022)), future studies could examine how predictions develop as a movement unfolds, how they change with practice, and how neural responses to the eventual outcome depend on the information already available.
text.formatted: Building on motor-control research <ref type="bibr">(Maurer et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Maurer et al., , 2022))</ref>, future studies could examine how predictions develop as a movement unfolds, how they change with practice, and how neural responses to the eventual outcome depend on the information already available.

text.text: This could help explain how anticipatory and outcome-related processes contribute jointly to the monitoring of continuous goal-directed behavior.
A further opportunity concerns the significance that events acquire through a player's goals and role.

Existing studies illustrate this through destination-dependent target relevance in a taxi-driving game (Weidemann et al., 2009) and different responses to events on a shared display in two-player games (Yokota et al., 2019; Fincham et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Existing studies illustrate this through destination-dependent target relevance in a taxi-driving game <ref type="bibr">(Weidemann et al., 2009)</ref> and different responses to events on a shared display in two-player games <ref type="bibr" target="#b218">(Yokota et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fincham et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: More systematic manipulations could examine how neural responses change when a physically identical event becomes relevant to one's own action, a teammate's performance, or a shared goal.
Such work could clarify how event-related activity reflects the relation between an event and the ongoing task, beyond its sensory properties.

Together, these directions could help establish where video game paradigms provide a useful connection between the experimental control of traditional laboratory tasks and the continuous, consequential, and socially situated behavior studied outside the laboratory.
Video games offer new opportunities to study the neural correlates of cognition during continuous, goal-directed behavior.

The current state of the literature suggests that game-elicited EEG responses show selective convergence with established laboratory effects, particularly for P3-like positivities sensitive to event probability, outcome magnitude, and player relevance, as well as for movement-related activity.
Clearly, the interpretation of these responses requires attention to methodological challenges such as precise event marking, overlapping neural activity, and context-dependent event properties.

These challenges notwithstanding, we believe that, compared with traditional cognitive event-related EEG research using highly simplified and abstract paradigms, combining video game play with event-related EEG research holds strong potential for elucidating the neural correlates of cognition in more complex and interactive settings with ever-increasing ecological validity.

text.text: Another common finding is an enhanced P3 component in response to no-go stimuli (no-go P3), typically peaking 300-600 ms post-stimulus, with a frontocentral distribution when compared to the parietal maximum observed for the go P3 (Falkenstein et al., 1999; Bruin, 2002; Gajewski and Falkenstein, 2013).

text.text: The N400 is a negative deflection beginning approximately 200-250 ms and peaking around 400 ms post-stimulus, with a broad centroparietal maximum and, for written words, a slight right-hemisphere bias (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).

text.text: It was first reported for semantically incongruent sentence-final words (e.g., He spread the warm bread with socks) and is typically quantified as the incongruent-minus-congruent difference, termed the N400 effect (Kutas and Hillyard, 1980; Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).
text.formatted: It was first reported for semantically incongruent sentence-final words (e.g., He spread the warm bread with socks) and is typically quantified as the incongruent-minus-congruent difference, termed the N400 effect <ref type="bibr">(Kutas and Hillyard, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kutas and Federmeier, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Semantic violations only represent the extreme of a graded continuum: every word elicits some N400 activity, and its amplitude decreases as the word becomes more expected in its context, whereas its latency remains largely stable (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).
text.formatted: Semantic violations only represent the extreme of a graded continuum: every word elicits some N400 activity, and its amplitude decreases as the word becomes more expected in its context, whereas its latency remains largely stable <ref type="bibr">(Kutas and Federmeier, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Although first characterized for words, N400 effects generalize to meaningful nonlinguistic stimuli, including line drawings, pictures, and visual scenes (Nigam et al., 1992; Ganis et al., 1996; Ganis and Kutas, 2003; Võ and Wolfe, 2013), visual narratives (Cohn and Kutas, 2015), and actions, gestures, and arithmetic problems (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).

text.text: The N400 is therefore thought to reflect the ease of accessing meaning from semantic memory in a given context, rather than language processing or violation detection per se (Kutas and Federmeier, 2011).

text.text: This broader sensitivity to meaningful stimuli provides context for interpretations involving violations of environmental expectations, but does not establish that every expectancy-related negativity is an N400.

Alpha and beta ERD/ERS In the time-frequency domain, stimulus-induced responses are commonly quantified as event-related desynchronization (ERD) and event-related synchronization (ERS), describing phasic changes in oscillatory power associated with internal or external events, conventionally considered in terms of non-phase-locked activity (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999).
text.formatted: Alpha and beta ERD/ERS In the time-frequency domain, stimulus-induced responses are commonly quantified as event-related desynchronization (ERD) and event-related synchronization (ERS), describing phasic changes in oscillatory power associated with internal or external events, conventionally considered in terms of non-phase-locked activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">(Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: More generally, event-related power estimates may include both phase-locked and non-phase-locked contributions, depending on the analysis.
Spectral measures should therefore not be assumed to isolate activity independent of the ERP.
ERD denotes a power decrease relative to a pre-event baseline, also referred to as blocking of a given rhythm, while ERS denotes a power increase.
Both phenomena are frequency-band-specific and characterized by a localized scalp topography.

Alpha ERD (8-13 Hz) is elicited across a broad range of task types, is topographically widespread, and is broadly interpreted as an electrophysiological correlate of activated cortical areas engaged in sensory or cognitive processing, with magnitude scaling with task demand (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999, 2017).
text.formatted: Alpha ERD (8-13 Hz) is elicited across a broad range of task types, is topographically widespread, and is broadly interpreted as an electrophysiological correlate of activated cortical areas engaged in sensory or cognitive processing, with magnitude scaling with task demand <ref type="bibr">(Pfurtscheller and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lopes da Silva, 1999, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In oddball paradigms, alpha ERD to target stimuli co-occurs with the P3 over similar scalp regions and exhibits comparable task sensitivity, suggesting that the two measures reflect associated or overlapping processes (Yordanova et al., 2001; Polich, 2007).
text.formatted: In oddball paradigms, alpha ERD to target stimuli co-occurs with the P3 over similar scalp regions and exhibits comparable task sensitivity, suggesting that the two measures reflect associated or overlapping processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b219">(Yordanova et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Polich, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Anticipatory alpha ERD may further be modality-specific, with occipitally maximal ERD preceding visual stimuli and temporally maximal ERD preceding auditory stimuli (Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017).
text.formatted: Anticipatory alpha ERD may further be modality-specific, with occipitally maximal ERD preceding visual stimuli and temporally maximal ERD preceding auditory stimuli <ref type="bibr">(Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Beta-band oscillations (13-30 Hz) have traditionally been studied in the context of sensorimotor tasks, where contralateral beta ERD over the motor cortex precedes voluntary movement and is followed by a post-movement beta ERS (see movement-related ERD/ERS discussed below; Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 1999).

Beyond their sensorimotor role, beta oscillations have increasingly been implicated in a range of cognitive functions, including working memory, top-down processing, and decision making (Spitzer and Haegens, 2017).
text.formatted: Beyond their sensorimotor role, beta oscillations have increasingly been implicated in a range of cognitive functions, including working memory, top-down processing, and decision making <ref type="bibr" target="#b201">(Spitzer and Haegens, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: RP and LRP Two of the most commonly studied response-locked ERPs are the readiness potential (RP) and the lateralized readiness potential (LRP) observed preceding voluntary movements.

The RP is characterized by a slowly increasing negative potential starting approximately 2 s before the onset of voluntary movement, recorded over central scalp sites and originating from central motor regions including pre-SMA, SMA proper, premotor cortex, and primary motor cortex (M1) (Libet et al., 1983; Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006).
text.formatted: The RP is characterized by a slowly increasing negative potential starting approximately 2 s before the onset of voluntary movement, recorded over central scalp sites and originating from central motor regions including pre-SMA, SMA proper, premotor cortex, and primary motor cortex (M1) <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">(Libet et al., 1983;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The RP can be divided into two distinct phases: an early RP component beginning approximately 2 s pre-movement with bilateral distribution, and a late RP starting approximately 400 ms pre-movement that becomes maximal over the contralateral M1 opposite the moving hand (Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006).
text.formatted: The RP can be divided into two distinct phases: an early RP component beginning approximately 2 s pre-movement with bilateral distribution, and a late RP starting approximately 400 ms pre-movement that becomes maximal over the contralateral M1 opposite the moving hand <ref type="bibr">(Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: The LRP is derived from differences between C3 and C4 activity calculated separately for leftand right-hand responses.
Its sign depends on the subtraction convention.
It typically emerges approximately 200 ms before movement onset (Trevena and Miller, 2002; Smulders and Miller, 2012).
text.formatted: It typically emerges approximately 200 ms before movement onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b205">(Trevena and Miller, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Smulders and Miller, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Movement-related ERD/ERS Voluntary movement is associated with ERD in the upper alpha band (10-12 Hz) and lower beta band (13-20 Hz), most prominently over sensorimotor areas, with ERD beginning before movement onset (Pfurtscheller and Aranibar, 1979; Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989; Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017).
text.formatted: Movement-related ERD/ERS Voluntary movement is associated with ERD in the upper alpha band (10-12 Hz) and lower beta band (13-20 Hz), most prominently over sensorimotor areas, with ERD beginning before movement onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">(Pfurtscheller and Aranibar, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Pre-movement alpha ERD begins with contralateral dominance and becomes bilateral shortly before movement execution, remaining almost symmetric during movement before recovering slowly over several seconds post-movement.

This pattern is assumed to reflect general readiness or presetting of neurons in motor and sensory areas required for movement execution (Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989; Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 2003).
text.formatted: This pattern is assumed to reflect general readiness or presetting of neurons in motor and sensory areas required for movement execution <ref type="bibr">(Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Beta ERD during execution is followed by rapid recovery and a characteristic short rebound (post-movement beta ERS ) within one second, with strict somatotopic organization and area-specific frequencies (e.g., hand area around 16-20 Hz and midcentral foot area around 20-24 Hz), suggested to reflect the shift of motor neurons from an activated to a deactivated state after movement termination or somatosensory processing (Pfurtscheller et al., 1996 (Pfurtscheller et al., , 1998;; Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 2003; Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017; Cassim et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Beta ERD during execution is followed by rapid recovery and a characteristic short rebound (post-movement beta ERS ) within one second, with strict somatotopic organization and area-specific frequencies (e.g., hand area around 16-20 Hz and midcentral foot area around 20-24 Hz), suggested to reflect the shift of motor neurons from an activated to a deactivated state after movement termination or somatosensory processing <ref type="bibr">(Pfurtscheller et al., 1996</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b187">(Pfurtscheller et al., , 1998;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b185">Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pfurtscheller and Lopes da Silva, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Cassim et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The error-related negativity (ERN; also termed error negativity, Ne) is a frontocentral negative deflection that emerges around the onset of an erroneous response and peaks approximately 50-100 ms post-response in speeded choice tasks such as flanker and choice reaction time tasks, with a maximum over midline frontocentral electrodes (Falkenstein et al., 1991; Gehring et al., 1993 Gehring et al., , 2012)).
text.formatted: The error-related negativity (ERN; also termed error negativity, Ne) is a frontocentral negative deflection that emerges around the onset of an erroneous response and peaks approximately 50-100 ms post-response in speeded choice tasks such as flanker and choice reaction time tasks, with a maximum over midline frontocentral electrodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">(Falkenstein et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">Gehring et al., 1993</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gehring et al., , 2012))</ref>.

text.text: It is quantified in response-locked averages, either as the errortrial waveform relative to correct trials or as an error-minus-correct difference wave, and has been observed across sensory modalities (visual, auditory, and tactile) and response effectors (manual, foot, oculomotor, and vocal) (Gehring et al., 2012).
text.formatted: It is quantified in response-locked averages, either as the errortrial waveform relative to correct trials or as an error-minus-correct difference wave, and has been observed across sensory modalities (visual, auditory, and tactile) and response effectors (manual, foot, oculomotor, and vocal) <ref type="bibr">(Gehring et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In conventional discrete-response tasks, the ERN emerges before external feedback about response accuracy and is thought to reflect error detection based on internal information about the executed response (Gehring et al., 1993; Holroyd and Coles, 2002).
text.formatted: In conventional discrete-response tasks, the ERN emerges before external feedback about response accuracy and is thought to reflect error detection based on internal information about the executed response <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">(Gehring et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Holroyd and Coles, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The distinction between internal and external information is less clear during continuous motor control, as discussed in the motor-domain subsection below.

A smaller negativity with similar latency and scalp distribution, the correct-response negativity (CRN), is sometimes also observed after correct responses, although whether the ERN and CRN reflect the same underlying process remains debated (Vidal et al., 2000; Gehring et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A smaller negativity with similar latency and scalp distribution, the correct-response negativity (CRN), is sometimes also observed after correct responses, although whether the ERN and CRN reflect the same underlying process remains debated <ref type="bibr">(Vidal et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Gehring et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The ERN is typically followed by the error positivity (Pe), a broad positive deflection beginning approximately 150-200 ms after the error and extending into the 200-500 ms range, usually with a centroparietal maximum, although its scalp distribution varies considerably across studies (Falkenstein et al., 2000; Overbeek et al., 2005).
text.formatted: The ERN is typically followed by the error positivity (Pe), a broad positive deflection beginning approximately 150-200 ms after the error and extending into the 200-500 ms range, usually with a centroparietal maximum, although its scalp distribution varies considerably across studies <ref type="bibr">(Falkenstein et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">Overbeek et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: The Pe, particularly its later subcomponent (400-600 ms), is associated with conscious error awareness, whereas the ERN occurs irrespective of whether errors are consciously perceived (Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001; Endrass et al., 2007).
text.formatted: The Pe, particularly its later subcomponent (400-600 ms), is associated with conscious error awareness, whereas the ERN occurs irrespective of whether errors are consciously perceived <ref type="bibr" target="#b174">(Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Endrass et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Together, the ERN and Pe are thought to reflect performance-monitoring processes that support behavioral adaptation (Ullsperger et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Together, the ERN and Pe are thought to reflect performance-monitoring processes that support behavioral adaptation <ref type="bibr">(Ullsperger et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: FRN, RewP and Feedback-related P3 Feedback-related electrophysiological responses are commonly characterized by an early frontocentral component peaking approximately 200-300 ms after feedback onset.

Historically, this component has been termed the feedback-related negativity (FRN; Miltner et al., 1997; Gehring and Willoughby, 2002), a negative deflection that is typically larger for unfavorable (punishing or unrewarding) than for favorable outcomes in gambling, time-estimation, and probabilistic learning tasks.
text.formatted: Historically, this component has been termed the feedback-related negativity (FRN; <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">Miltner et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">Gehring and Willoughby, 2002)</ref>, a negative deflection that is typically larger for unfavorable (punishing or unrewarding) than for favorable outcomes in gambling, time-estimation, and probabilistic learning tasks.

text.text: More recent work suggests that this apparent negativity may instead reflect a common N2-like response on which a reward-related positivity, the reward positivity (RewP; Holroyd et al., 2008; Foti et al., 2011; Proudfit, 2015), is superimposed.
text.formatted: More recent work suggests that this apparent negativity may instead reflect a common N2-like response on which a reward-related positivity, the reward positivity (RewP; <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Holroyd et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">Foti et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">Proudfit, 2015)</ref>, is superimposed.

text.text: The RewP is elicited by rewarding outcomes and is reduced or absent following non-rewards, giving rise to the apparent FRN difference between outcome types.
Whether the FRN and RewP reflect distinct components or alternative descriptions of the same process remains debated, and studies differ in how they quantify and label them.
One approach refers to the negative waveform following unfavorable outcomes as the FRN and to the positive waveform following favorable outcomes as the RewP.

Another computes difference waves between outcome types, in which subtracting rewards from non-rewards yields a negative deflection (FRN) and the reverse contrast yields a positive deflection (RewP) (Proudfit, 2015; Krigolson, 2018).
text.formatted: Another computes difference waves between outcome types, in which subtracting rewards from non-rewards yields a negative deflection (FRN) and the reverse contrast yields a positive deflection (RewP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">(Proudfit, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krigolson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: FRN/RewP amplitude is sensitive to outcome probability and magnitude, with larger responses reported for unexpected or lower-probability outcomes and for outcomes of higher magnitude (Sambrook and Goslin, 2015; Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: FRN/RewP amplitude is sensitive to outcome probability and magnitude, with larger responses reported for unexpected or lower-probability outcomes and for outcomes of higher magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Sambrook and Goslin, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These effects should be interpreted in relation to the task and the way the component is quantified, rather than as invariant properties.

The FRN/RewP is typically followed by a feedback-related P3, more specifically the P3b, which peaks approximately 300-600 ms after feedback onset with a centroparietal scalp distribution (Polich, 2007; Walentowska et al., 2016; Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The FRN/RewP is typically followed by a feedback-related P3, more specifically the P3b, which peaks approximately 300-600 ms after feedback onset with a centroparietal scalp distribution <ref type="bibr">(Polich, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Walentowska et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Its amplitude has been linked to outcome evaluation and is often larger for rewards than for non-rewards, for unexpected or lowprobability outcomes, and for outcomes of higher magnitude (Hajcak et al., 2005; Glazer et al., 2018; Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020; Paul et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Its amplitude has been linked to outcome evaluation and is often larger for rewards than for non-rewards, for unexpected or lowprobability outcomes, and for outcomes of higher magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Hajcak et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Glazer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Stewardson and Sambrook, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Paul et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The ERN and FRN share a frontocentral scalp distribution, and source-localization and neuroimaging evidence points to a common generator in the medial frontal cortex, most notably the anterior cingulate cortex (Miltner et al., 1997; Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Holroyd et al., 2004; Gehring et al., 2012; Walsh and Anderson, 2012) but they differ in latency and time-locking convention.
text.formatted: The ERN and FRN share a frontocentral scalp distribution, and source-localization and neuroimaging evidence points to a common generator in the medial frontal cortex, most notably the anterior cingulate cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">(Miltner et al., 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Holroyd and Coles, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">Holroyd et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Gehring et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Walsh and Anderson, 2012)</ref> but they differ in latency and time-locking convention.

text.text: According to the reinforcement learning theory of Holroyd and Coles (2002), both components reflect a reward prediction error signal, conveyed by the midbrain dopamine system to the anterior cingulate cortex, indicating that an outcome is worse than expected (see also Nieuwenhuis et al., 2004; Walsh and Anderson, 2012).
text.formatted: According to the reinforcement learning theory of <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">Holroyd and Coles (2002)</ref>, both components reflect a reward prediction error signal, conveyed by the midbrain dopamine system to the anterior cingulate cortex, indicating that an outcome is worse than expected (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">Nieuwenhuis et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Walsh and Anderson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The two components are thought to differ primarily in the information on which this evaluation is based and, consequently, in the event to which they are time-locked.

The ERN (time-locked to action or response) emerges after movement and prior to external feedback and reflects an evaluation based on internal information about the executed response, whereas the FRN (timelocked to external outcome feedback) reflects an evaluation based on external feedback (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Walsh and Anderson, 2012; Krigolson, 2018).
text.formatted: The ERN (time-locked to action or response) emerges after movement and prior to external feedback and reflects an evaluation based on internal information about the executed response, whereas the FRN (timelocked to external outcome feedback) reflects an evaluation based on external feedback <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Holroyd and Coles, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Walsh and Anderson, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Krigolson, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Some studies indicate that their relative contribution depends on how much information about the outcome is available before feedback.
The ERN is larger when the response determines the outcome, and the FRN when it does not (Holroyd and Coles, 2002; Walsh and Anderson, 2012).
text.formatted: The ERN is larger when the response determines the outcome, and the FRN when it does not <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Holroyd and Coles, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">Walsh and Anderson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As stimulus-response mappings are learned, the error signal can accordingly shift from the feedback to the response.

Frontal midline theta activity, which accompanies both components, has been proposed as a common mid-frontal mechanism signaling the need for control across these and related events (Cavanagh et al., 2012).

text.text: Feedback-related time-frequency components Feedback processing is also accompanied by modulations of oscillatory activity (for reviews, see Luft, 2014; Glazer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Feedback-related time-frequency components Feedback processing is also accompanied by modulations of oscillatory activity (for reviews, see <ref type="bibr">Luft, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Glazer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: One commonly reported modulation is an increase in frontal midline theta power (4-8 Hz) approximately 200-500 ms after unfavorable outcomes or negative performance feedback, maximal over Fz and FCz (Cohen et al., 2007; Marco-Pallares et al., 2008; Cavanagh et al., 2010; Van De Vijver et al., 2011).
text.formatted: One commonly reported modulation is an increase in frontal midline theta power (4-8 Hz) approximately 200-500 ms after unfavorable outcomes or negative performance feedback, maximal over Fz and FCz <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">(Cohen et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b165">Marco-Pallares et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Cavanagh et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b207">Van De Vijver et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Frontal midline theta is thought to originate in or near the anterior cingulate cortex and to contribute to the FRN.

It has been linked to performance monitoring and reinforcement learning, as it scales with reward prediction errors and predicts behavioral adjustment and individual differences in learning (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Van De Vijver et al., 2011; Luft et al., 2013).
text.formatted: It has been linked to performance monitoring and reinforcement learning, as it scales with reward prediction errors and predicts behavioral adjustment and individual differences in learning <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b207">Van De Vijver et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Luft et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Its sensitivity, however, is not restricted to negative outcomes.

Because frontal midline theta has been found to be also modulated by novelty, conflict, and errors alike, it has been proposed to reflect a domain-general mechanism that signals the need for cognitive control (Cavanagh et al., 2012; Cavanagh and Frank, 2014).
text.formatted: Because frontal midline theta has been found to be also modulated by novelty, conflict, and errors alike, it has been proposed to reflect a domain-general mechanism that signals the need for cognitive control <ref type="bibr">(Cavanagh et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Cavanagh and Frank, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Beta activity (13-30 Hz) has been reported to increase after positive feedback and desynchronize after negative feedback over frontal and central sites, within approximately 200-600 ms after feedback onset (Cohen et al., 2007; Marco-Pallares et al., 2008; Van De Vijver et al., 2011; Luft et al., 2013).

text.text: Two forms of feedback-related beta have been distinguished (Luft, 2014).
text.formatted: Two forms of feedback-related beta have been distinguished <ref type="bibr">(Luft, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: One is a frontal increase in the beta and low-gamma range after rewards, particularly unexpected ones (Marco-Pallares et al., 2008; HajiHosseini et al., 2012).

text.text: The other is a sensorimotor beta response to performance feedback in motor tasks, which increases after correct feedback and decreases after errors (Van De Vijver et al., 2011; Luft et al., 2013).
text.formatted: The other is a sensorimotor beta response to performance feedback in motor tasks, which increases after correct feedback and decreases after errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b207">(Van De Vijver et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">Luft et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Feedback-related beta has accordingly been interpreted both as a reward or learning signal (Marco-Pallarés et al., 2015; Luft, 2014) and as a signal for maintaining or adjusting the current motor state (Engel and Fries, 2010).

text.text: Owing to its sensorimotor topography, the second form also overlaps with the movement-related beta ERD/ERS described above.

Feedback-locked delta power (below approximately 4 Hz), maximal over parietal sites approximately 100-500 ms after feedback onset, has been reported to be larger after gains than after losses (Bernat et al., 2015; Cavanagh, 2015).

text.text: Time-frequency decompositions indicate that it contributes predominantly to the feedback-related P3, and in part to the RewP (Bernat et al., 2015).

text.text: Event-locked alpha modulations have received comparatively little attention in feedback paradigms.
Where reported, alpha decreases are commonly interpreted, as in other contexts, as reflecting cortical activation and attentional engagement (see Alpha and beta ERD/ERS above, Glazer et al., 2018).
